name: Puftaloon
summary: A puftaloon is a shallow-fried scone of Australian origin.
fun_fact_candidates: Puftaloons can be served with sweet or savoury accompaniments, although they were traditionally eaten with golden syrup or treacle.
Puftaloons are also known as fried scones and were historically called moon balls, puff de lunas, and puftaloonies.
Puftaloons continued to be eaten through the early 20th century.
During the Great Depression of the 1930s when food was scarce, puftaloons were considered a rare treat, eaten with golden syrup known under the nickname "cocky's joy".

sources.name: Wikipedia: List of New Zealand dishes

name: Pumpkin scone
summary: Pumpkin scones are an Australian version of the scone containing mashed pumpkin, and are among the best-known of the desserts that originate from Australia.
fun_fact_candidates: Pumpkin scones were likely developed in Queensland.
They are first recorded in a cookbook in 1922, in Australian Home Cookery, though recipes had been around for at least a decade.

The earliest identified in the Queensland History Journal came in 1912 from a Beatrice McNicol of Mitchell, Queensland, who included "3 cups flour, ½ cup sugar, ½ cup milk, 1 tabs butter, ½ teas salt, 1 cup mashed pumpkin, 1 teaspoon bicarbonate of soda, 2 teaspoons cream of tartar".

By 1916, the pumpkin scone was well-established in Queensland baking competitions, and was appearing in mentions outside of the state, including a recipe published in Kalgoorlie, a city in rural Western Australia.

Pumpkins had long been a common element of the Australian diet following their import from the Americas via Britain, but it was in the 1920s, following the development of the Queensland Blue and Triamble varieties, that they became ubiquitous in Australian cooking.

Despite the scone variety consistently being most popular in Queensland, they were eaten across the country, as attested to in an article from the Sydney Morning Herald on 10 March 1924, reporting on the Manning River Show: "there were... 78 entries in scones.

They at least should be an economical product of the kitchen on the north coast, where almost every cultivated field has its wide spreading pumpkin vines." Through the 1920s and 1930s, recipes for pumpkin scones, alongside pumpkin soups, fritters, and cakes appeared throughout newspapers.
From 1936, pumpkin scones were included on the curriculum of primary school home economics classes in Queensland state schools, ensuring the dish remained relevant in the state.

sources.name: Wikipedia: List of New Zealand dishes

name: Rissole
summary: A rissole (from Latin russeolus, meaning reddish, via French rissoler, meaning "to redden") is "a ball or flattened cake of chopped meat, fish or vegetables mixed with herbs or spices, then coated in breadcrumbs and fried."

sources.name: Wikipedia: List of New Zealand dishes

name: Rocky road (dessert)
summary: Rocky road is a candy, made up of various ingredients—typically including nuts, marshmallows, and dried fruit—that are combined with melted chocolate and left to set.
fun_fact_candidates: In America, rocky road is most popular as an ice cream flavor.

The earliest recipe for rocky road found by the cookbook author Jean Anderson came in Young America’s Cookbook, a 1938 publication of the New York Herald Tribune, though she identifies a potential precursor in a recipe for "Chocolate Marshmallow Fudge" in the 1923 edition of The Boston Cooking-School Cook Book.

The food blog Australian Food Timeline traces the earliest mentions of rocky road to around this time in America, with the earliest being a 1920 reference to "Rocky Road Creams" in Santa Cruz, California.
The 1920s were the period that the first rocky road ice creams are claimed to have been invented.

summary: Rēwena bread or Māori bread (Māori: parāoa rēwena; literally 'flour leaven') is a type of sourdough bread from New Zealand.
fun_fact_candidates: It originated amongst the Māori people and is closely associated with Māori cuisine.

sources.name: Wikipedia: List of New Zealand dishes

name: Sausage sizzle
sections: New Zealand foods > Imported foods, now significant in New Zealand
summary: A sausage sizzle is a community event originating from either Australia or New Zealand to cook and serve sausages in bread (also referred to as sausage sandwiches or sausage sizzles), which are grilled or barbecued sausages (most commonly beef or pork) served in sliced bread with grilled onions and various condiments, most commonly tomato sauce, barbecue sauce or mustard.
fun_fact_candidates: The term "sausage sizzle" came into common use in the 1980s and is used primarily to refer to the barbecuing event, but also to the sausage itself, mostly in Western Australia.
Fundraising sausage sizzles have become particularly associated with elections in Australia (colloquially known as a democracy sausage) and the hardware chain Bunnings.

name: Saveloy
summary: A saveloy is a type of highly seasoned sausage, usually bright red, normally boiled and available in fish and chip shops around Britain.
story_candidates: The word is believed to be derived from Middle French cervelas or servelat, originating from Old Italian cervella ('pigs brains'), ultimately from the Latin cerebrum ('brain').
Its first known use in the English language in this meaning was 1784.

name: Seasoned salt
summary: Seasoned salt is a blend of table salt, herbs, spices, other flavourings, and sometimes monosodium glutamate (MSG).

name: Slippery Bob
summary: Slippery Bob is a historical dish made by frying kangaroo brains in emu fat.
fun_fact_candidates: It is among the best known of Abbott's recipes―writing at the end of the 20th century, the food historian Barbara Santich describes Slippery Bob as part of a national mythology alongside damper and pan jam, assuming a place in Australia like the bunyip.

name: Solo (Australian soft drink)
summary: Solo is an Australian, lemon-flavoured, carbonated soft drink currently manufactured under license by Asahi Breweries.
fun_fact_candidates: First launched by Tarax in 1968 and fell to Cadbury after a takeover in 1974, its lemon flavour is inspired by Australian pubs' traditional and popular non-alcoholic 'pub squash' beverage.
There is also an energy drink version called ‘Solo Energy’, released approximately in June 2025.
story_candidates: Solo was first launched by Tarax in 1968, then Cadbury-Schweppes took over in 1973.
In April 2009, Asahi acquired Cadbury-Schweppes Australia and in turn Solo.
The drink's lemon flavour is derived from Australian pubs' traditional non-alcoholic beverage 'pub squash' or 'lemon squash', which is a drink made from a sweetened lemon concentrate and water.
In response to concerns associated with high sugar content, Asahi beverages and subsequently Solo signed a sugar reduction pledge in 2018.
Solo aims to reduce its sugar content by 20% by the year 2025.
Solo Energy, an energy drink range with guarana, caffeine and B-vitamins, was released in June 2025.

name: Steak sandwich (Australia)
summary: In Australian cuisine, a steak sandwich is a dish consisting of a steak on a bun, roll, or between slices of bread, often with a variety of other ingredients.

name: Surf and turf
sections: Main dishes > Fast food, pub meals
summary: Surf and turf, sometimes called reef and beef, is a main course typically served at steakhouses combining seafood and red meat, usually beefsteak.
story_candidates: While the term's origins remain unclear, the earliest known use of the phrase in print dates to 1961 in the Los Angeles Times.
In late 19th-century America, combining large portions of lobster and steak was popular at "show restaurants known as lobster palaces", favored by nouveau riche "arrivistes".
This became unfashionable by the 1920s and only regained popularity in the early 1960s.
Surf 'n' turf was featured in 1962 at the Eye of the Needle, a revolving restaurant atop the Space Needle in Seattle, Washington.
Surf and turf is often considered to symbolize the middle-class "Continental cuisine" of the 1960s and 1970s, with (frozen) lobster and steak as replacements for the middle class.
In Australia, the dish was first served in 1965 at the Lithgow Hotel in Lithgow, New South Wales.

name: Tomato sauce
summary: Tomato sauce can refer to many different sauces made primarily from tomatoes.
fun_fact_candidates: In dishes tomato sauces are common for meat and vegetables such as in stews, but they are perhaps best known as bases for Italian pasta or pizza dishes, or in Mexican salsas.
story_candidates: Bernardino de Sahagún, a Franciscan friar from the Kingdom of Spain, is believed to be the first European to write about tomato sauce after encountering it for sale in the markets of Tenochtitlan (today Mexico City).

The first Italian recipe of tomato sauce was published under the name "Spanish tomato sauce" in Lo Scalco alla Moderna ('The Modern Steward'), written by Italian chef Antonio Latini and published in two volumes in 1692 and 1694.
Here is where we find the first mention of tomatoes being mixed with olive oil, onion, garlic, chili, and herbs.
The Provençals who went to Paris for the National Federation Day of July 14, 1790, demanded tomatoes everywhere they went.
The use of tomato sauce with pasta appeared for the first time in 1790 in the Italian cookbook L'Apicio moderno, by Roman chef Francesco Leonardi.
The first written recipe for canned tomatoes comes from Vaucluse, in southern France; it appears in a document written by an individual in 1795.

sources.name: Wikipedia: List of New Zealand dishes

name: Vanilla slice
summary: Vanilla slice is an Australian pastry comprising a thick layer of vanilla custard sandwiched between puff pastry and topped with icing sugar or a thin layer of icing.
fun_fact_candidates: Similar varieties of the dessert exist in Europe and North America, and it is believed to have evolved from one of the similar European desserts.
story_candidates: Most notably this includes the Mille-feuille, which is believed to have originated in France.
It is believed that the Australian vanilla slice emerged as a variety of one of these similar desserts, but it is unknown which variety or varieties evolved into the modern vanilla slice.

In keeping with the informality and disdain for pretence in Australian vernacular, it is common to refer to the dessert using colloquial names based on bodily fluids such as pus, phlegm, or nasal mucus which are similar in appearance to the custard filling.
To celebrate its cultural significance, an annual competition known as The Great Australian Vanilla Slice Triumph has been held since 1998.
The event was hosted annually in Ouyen until 2001, when it moved to the nearby town of Merbein.

sources.name: Wikipedia: List of New Zealand dishes

name: Vegemite
sections: New Zealand foods > Imported foods, now significant in New Zealand
summary: Vegemite () is a brand of a thick, dark brown Australian food spread made from leftover brewers' yeast extract with various vegetable and spice additives.
fun_fact_candidates: It was developed by Cyril Callister in Melbourne, Victoria, for the Fred Walker Company in 1922 and was first sold in stores on 25 October 1923.
Following the death of Fred Walker in 1935, the Vegemite brand came under the ownership of the American company Kraft Foods.
However, in 2017 the brand returned to Australian ownership when the Bega Group purchased it alongside other assets from Mondelez International (formerly Kraft Foods Inc.).
story_candidates: The Australian rock band Men at Work refer to a "Vegemite sandwich" in the second verse of their 1982 hit song "Down Under", from their debut studio album Business as Usual.

Australian band King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard have a song called "Vegemite" on their 2014 album Oddments. "True Blue", a country music song written by Australian singer-songwriter John Williamson, mentions Vegemite.

sources.name: Wikipedia: List of New Zealand dishes

name: Wafer
summary: A wafer is a crisp, often sweet, very thin, flat, light biscuit, often used to decorate ice cream, and also used as a garnish on some sweet dishes.

sources.name: Wikipedia: List of New Zealand dishes

name: Wagon Wheels
summary: Wagon Wheels are a sweet snack food sold in the United Kingdom as well as other Commonwealth countries such as Australia, Canada, New Zealand, Malta and India.
fun_fact_candidates: Wagon Wheels were invented by William Peschardt, who sold the patent to Garry Weston, son of W. Garfield Weston.
The name (originally "Weston Wagon Wheels") relates to the shape of the biscuits and capitalised on the Wild West, which was popular in mass media at the time.
story_candidates: Wagon Wheels were chosen by Judge Paul Hollywood as the technical challenge for the first episode in series 9 of The Great British Bake Off.

Australian interviewer Annabel Crabb fabricated a batch of Wagon Wheels as her contribution to an interview with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at The Lodge in her ABC series Kitchen Cabinet, first aired in July 2026.

sources.name: Wikipedia: List of New Zealand dishes

name: Weet-Bix
sections: New Zealand foods > Imported foods, now significant in New Zealand
summary: Weet-Bix is a whole-grain wheat breakfast cereal created and manufactured in Australia and New Zealand by the Sanitarium Health Food Company, and in South Africa by Bokomo.
story_candidates: In the mid-1910s, Bennison Osborne set out to develop an improved version of Granose, a biscuit sold by the Seventh-day Adventist Church through the for-profit Sanitarium Health Food Company.
On 19 August 1926, he applied for a trademark for his biscuit, having named it Weet-Bix.
In October 1928, Weet-Bix a success, Shannon sold the rights to Sanitarium, specifically Australasian Conference Association Limited.
The British & African Cereal Company, Ltd. was registered in London in 1932, as a private company, with the proprietor shown as Weetabix Limited of Weetabix Mills, Kettering.
All shares in the company were specified to be under the control of the directors, the first of whom were Osborne, Macfarlane, Alfred Richard Upton and Arthur Stanley Scrutton.
For the purpose of legally differentiating the product from that sold in Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, the product was named Weetabix.
In 1933, Macfarlane left the company to pursue other business interests, leaving Osborne as the sole managing director.
Osborne sold his shareholding to the directors in July 1936, at which time the company was renamed Weetabix Limited.
Weet-Bix Clusters were discontinued in June 2025.

sources.name: Wikipedia: List of New Zealand dishes

name: White Christmas (food)
summary: White Christmas is an Australian dessert made from dried fruit such as sultanas, glacé cherries, desiccated coconut, icing sugar, milk powder and Rice Bubbles, with hydrogenated coconut oil (such as the brand Copha) as the binding ingredient.
fun_fact_candidates: It is a popular Christmas food item, especially as it can easily be made by children.

name: Whitebait
summary: Whitebait is a collective term for the immature fry of fish, typically between 25 and 50 millimetres (1 and 2 in) long.

sources.name: Wikipedia: List of New Zealand dishes

name: Witchetty grub
summary: The witchetty grub (also spelled witchety grub or witjuti grub) is a term used in Australia for the large, white, wood-eating larvae of several moths.

name: Worcestershire sauce
summary: Worcestershire sauce or Worcester sauce ( WUUS-tər(-shər)) is a fermented condiment invented by the pharmacists John Wheeley Lea and William Henry Perrins in Worcester, Worcestershire, England, during the first half of the 19th century.
fun_fact_candidates: Worcestershire sauce has been a generic term since 1876, when the High Court of Justice ruled that Lea & Perrins did not own a trademark for the name "Worcestershire".
story_candidates: The Lea & Perrins brand was commercialised in 1837 and was the first sauce to bear the Worcestershire name.

The company has also claimed that "Lord Sandys, ex-Governor of Bengal" encountered it while in India with the East India Company in the 1830s, and commissioned the local pharmacists (the partnership of John Wheeley Lea and William Perrins of 63 Broad Street, Worcester) to recreate it.
However, neither Marcus Lord Sandys nor any Baron Sandys was ever a Governor of Bengal, nor had they ever visited India as far as available records indicate.
According to company lore, when the recipe was first mixed, the resulting product was so strong that it was considered inedible and the barrel was abandoned in the basement.
In 1838, the first bottles of Lea & Perrins Worcestershire sauce were released to the general public.

sources.name: Wikipedia: List of New Zealand dishes

name: Zucchini slice
summary: Zucchini slice is a dish common in Australia and New Zealand that bears similarities to frittatas and quick breads.
fun_fact_candidates: It is one of a category of similarly-named and -served dishes common in the region, both sweet and savory.

sources.name: Wikipedia: List of New Zealand dishes

name: Beuschel
summary: Beuschel (German: [ˈbɔʏʃl̩] ) is a dish that is typically a ragout made from lungs and other organs, such as heart, kidneys, spleen, and tongue, from calf, beef, pork, or game.
story_candidates: In Austrian hunting terminology, the term refers to the lungs, liver, heart, spleen, and kidneys of game, known as the "hunter's right." According to the Duden, the word dates back to the early meaning of "Bausch" (swelling), which was used to refer to entrails.

Beuschel, also known as Beuschl, Beuscherl, Saures Lüngerl, Lungensuppe, or Lungenhaschee, refers to a dish in traditional Viennese, Austrian, Bavarian, and Bohemian cuisine (where it is known as pajšl).
Traditional restaurants in Bavaria and Austria often offer beuschel based on their own handed-down recipes.
In Swiss cuisine, a calf heart and lung ragout is known as Gschtell, according to the Swiss kitchen encyclopedia Chuchi-Dix.

In Upper Franconia, the dish is called Saure Lunge mit Herz or Gschling because it is prepared with vinegar or wine, while in Coburg, it is known as "Gelüng." Beuschel can be made from nearly all lungs and other organs such as heart, tongue, and kidney from cattle, pigs, or game.
Traditionally, it is prepared as a ragout from calf lungs, sometimes supplemented with heart, spleen, liver, and/or tongue, depending on the recipe.

Originally, innards, including beuschel, were served as a starter before the main course, known as "Voressen." The classic side dishes in Austria are either bread or napkin dumplings, while in Franconia, potato dumplings or Baumwollene Klöße ("cotton dumplings"), along with green salad, are common.

name: Einspänner
summary: An Einspänner is a Viennese coffee drink consisting of espresso ("Mocca" in Viennese terminology) topped with whipped cream.
fun_fact_candidates: It is traditionally served in a glass rather than a mug or a coffee cup.
story_candidates: The drink's name refers to the carriages that were common in Vienna in the 19th century, as it was intended for the drivers.
The Einspänner also found popularity beyond carriage drivers and quickly became a staple of Vienna's coffee houses.

name: Germknödel
summary: Germknödel (Austrian German pronunciation: [ˈɡɛɐ̯mˌknøːdl̩]) is a sweet, fluffy, yeast dough dumpling (Knödel), filled with spiced plum jam, topped with a mix of poppy seeds and sugar, and served with melted butter.
fun_fact_candidates: It is occasionally, even though less traditional, served with vanilla cream sauce instead.
It is considered a Mehlspeise or 'flour dish', popular with both Catholics during Lent and Jews.

name: Marillenknödel
summary: Marillenknödel (German: [maˈʁɪlənˌknøːdl̩] ; Czech: meruňkové knedlíky, lit. apricot dumplings) is a dessert common in Austrian (especially Viennese), Czech, and Hungarian cuisines, and across Central Europe.
fun_fact_candidates: Ferdinand I of Austria famously ordered Marillenknödel when apricots were out of season, to which he replied, "I am the Emperor and I want dumplings!"

name: Milk
summary: Milk is usually a white liquid food (but can be shades of yellow, cream, pink, or brown) produced by the mammary glands of lactating mammals.
fun_fact_candidates: The first milk, which is called colostrum, contains antibodies and immune-modulating components that strengthen the immune system against many diseases.
In 2011, dairy farms produced around 730 million tonnes (800 million short tons) of milk from 260 million dairy cows.
story_candidates: Humans first learned to consume the milk of other mammals regularly following the domestication of animals during the Neolithic Revolution or the development of agriculture.
Though the first evidence of the shift from meat production to milk production, appeared in Western Anatolia in the form of milk residue on pottery shards dated to circ. 6500 BC.

People first domesticated the most important dairy animals – cattle, sheep and goats – in Southwest Asia, although domestic cattle had been independently derived from wild aurochs populations several times since.

Sherratt's model is not supported by recent findings, based on the analysis of lipid residue in prehistoric pottery, that shows that dairying was practiced in the early phases of agriculture in Southwest Asia, by at least the seventh millennium BC.
The first farmers in central Europe and Britain milked their animals.
Sheep and goats were introduced to Africa from Southwest Asia, but African cattle may have been independently domesticated around 7000–6000 BC.
The earliest Egyptian records of burn treatments describe burn dressings using milk from mothers of male babies.
Incorrectly thought to be blood diverted from the womb to the breast, it was also known as "white blood", and treated like blood for religious dietary purposes and in humoral theory.
Cows were imported to New England in 1624.
In Greek mythology, the Milky Way was formed after the trickster god Hermes suckled the infant Heracles at the breast of Hera, the queen of the gods, while she was asleep.

name: Milk-cream strudel
summary: The milk-cream strudel (Viennese German: Millirahmstrudel; Standard German: Milchrahmstrudel) is a traditional Viennese strudel and a popular pastry in Austria and many countries in Europe that once belonged to the Austro-Hungarian Empire (1867–1918).
story_candidates: The first documented strudel recipe was a recipe of a milk-cream strudel (Millirahmstrudel) from 1696 in Vienna, a handwritten recipe at the Viennese City Library.

A Viennese legend credits Franz Stelzer (1842–1913), who owned a small inn in Breitenfurt near Vienna, for the invention of the Millirahmstrudel, maintaining that the pastry made him a very famous and rich man.

name: Powidl
summary: A powidl (also porvidl, powidła, povidla, or powidel) is a plum butter, a type of fruit spread prepared from the prune plum, that is popular in Central Europe.
fun_fact_candidates: The plums used should be harvested as late as possible, ideally after the first frosts, in order to ensure they contain enough sugar.
Powidl will keep for a long time, especially if kept in traditional crockery.
Traditionally, large amounts of powidl to be used as a winter store and natural sweetener were prepared in late autumn during a communal event.
Traditionally the plums were "overcooked," (to promote evaporation) in a copper kettle, or sometimes vinegar preserved, or even steamed.
Another recipe for "traditional Austrian plum butter" recommends roasting the plums in an oven and then transforming that compote-like dish into jam.
Powidl is a key ingredient of the popular Austrian street food pofesen, which is a jam-filled form of French toast.
story_candidates: In this the traditional method of production allows for a long shelf life even in unsealed containers.
The prune trees are less sensitive to cold, making them popular in harsher climate areas.
The high-sugar content, combined with good availability and storability, made Powidl into the general sweetener in many traditional recipes.

name: Wiener Melange
summary: A Melange (or Wiener Melange - "Vienna blend") is a specialty coffee drink similar to a cappuccino.

name: Aalsterse vla
sections: Belgian cuisine > Sweet dishes and desserts
summary: Aalsterse vla (also spelled Aalsterse vlaai) is a traditional pie from Belgium, originating from the city and surrounding region of Aalst in East Flanders, Belgium.
story_candidates: The exact origins of Aalsterse vla are unknown, but historical references to similar bread-based pies in Flanders date back to the 16th century.
It is believed to have originated as a way to use leftover bread, especially during festive periods.
Until the early 20th century, families without home ovens would bring the prepared dough to local bakeries to be baked.
In 2020, efforts began in Aalst to recognise the pie as part of Flanders’ intangible cultural heritage, supported by local baker guilds.

name: Algérienne sauce
summary: Algérienne sauce or Algerian sauce is a sweet and spicy sauce with a yellowish-orange color.
story_candidates: Sauce algérienne is mentioned in the 1876 book Le livre des menus authored by Fin-Bec.
Ernest Loewer describes the Algerian sauce in 1962 as comprising half-sautéed tomatoes, stuffed with a julienne of peppers, and served alongside croquette potatoes.

name: Babelutte
sections: Belgian cuisine > Sweet dishes and desserts
summary: A Babelutte is a sort of long toffee flavoured with honey or vergeoise (demerara sugar) from Veurne, in Westhoek (West Flanders, Belgium).
story_candidates: The candy originates from the 19th century, from a couple that prepared and sold it to tourists on Belgian coastal beaches.

name: Boulets à la Liégeoise
summary: The boulet à la liégeoise (French pronunciation: [bulɛ a la ljeʒwaz]; or more regionally called boulet sauce lapin, boulet (sauce) chasseur, or Boulets) is a Belgian dish made from balls of mixed minced pork and beef in a sauce containing Liège syrup.

learn_more.title: Books about Boulets à la Liégeoise (Open Library)

name: Cocktail sauce
summary: Cocktail sauce, also known as seafood sauce, is a cold or room temperature sauce served with seafood cocktail or as a condiment with other seafoods.
fun_fact_candidates: Seafood with such spiced, cold sauces was common in 19th and 20th century American cuisine.

name: Cougnou
sections: Belgian cuisine > Sweet dishes and desserts
summary: The cougnou or bread of Jesus is a Viennoiserie baked during Christmas time and is typical of the southern Low Countries.
fun_fact_candidates: This bread seems to have originated in ancient Hainaut but it is now spread throughout the southern Low Countries.

name: Couque de Dinant
summary: The Couque de Dinant (English: Cake of Dinant) is an extremely hard, sweet biscuit native to the southern Belgian city of Dinant in Wallonia.
story_candidates: A popular though unlikely legend holds that the couques arose from the sacking of Dinant in 1466 by Charles the Bold in the Liège Wars.
As the dough was so firm, they had the idea of printing it in the negative in dinanderie (local ornate brasswork), and thereby began the tradition of giving them patterns.
Much more certain is that the couque began to appear some time in the 18th century, though the exact circumstances of its invention are unclear.

learn_more.title: Books about Couque de Dinant (Open Library)

name: Cuberdon
sections: Belgian cuisine > Sweet dishes and desserts
summary: A cuberdon is a cone-shaped Belgian candy and a popular local delicacy in Ghent.
fun_fact_candidates: In Dutch it is also known as a neus ("nose"), Gentse neus ("Ghent nose"), or neuzeke ("little nose") for its likeness to a human nose.
Cuberdons are traditionally made with gum arabic candy crust with a soft, raspberry-flavored filling.
They are traditionally about 2.5 cm (1 inch) wide and weigh approximately 10 to 18 grams (0.35 to 0.63 oz), although smaller versions are also produced.
story_candidates: In 1873, pharmacist De Vynck in the city of Ghent discovered the recipe of the cuberdon by chance.

name: Curry ketchup
summary: Curry ketchup is a spiced variant of tomato ketchup and a common condiment in Belgium, Germany, the Netherlands and Scandinavia.
fun_fact_candidates: In Germany, it is sometimes used as a simple alternative to curry sauce, a sauce used for the dish currywurst, one of the most popular in the country.

name: Dame blanche (dessert)
sections: Belgian cuisine > Sweet dishes and desserts
summary: Dame blanche (French, "fair lady" and literally, "white lady") is the name used in Belgium and the Netherlands for a sweet dessert consisting of vanilla ice cream with whipped cream and warm molten chocolate.
fun_fact_candidates: In Germany and in Switzerland, the same type of dessert is known as a Coupe Dänemark.
The dish that was created by Auguste Escoffier originally consisted of almond milk ice cream, poached peach, lemon sorbet and white currants.

name: Dubbel
summary: The term dubbel (also double) is a Belgian Trappist beer naming convention.
fun_fact_candidates: The origin of the dubbel was a strong version of a brown beer brewed in Westmalle Abbey in 1856, which is known to have been on sale to the public by June 1861.
In 1926, the recipe was changed by brewer Henrik Verlinden, and it was sold as Dubbel Bruin.
Following World War II, abbey beers became popular in Belgium and the name "dubbel" was used by several breweries for commercial purposes.
Abbey 1856 Dubbel is produced in Argentina.

name: Filet américain
summary: Filet américain (often shortened to américain) a raw beef preparation associated particularly with Belgian cuisine and closely related to steak tartare.
story_candidates: Filet américain is associated particularly with Belgian brasserie and butcher traditions and is commonly served as a sandwich filling, starter or main dish, often with fries.

name: Flemish stew
summary: Flemish stew, known in Dutch as stoofvlees (pronounced [ˈstoːfleːs] ) or stoverij and in French as carbon(n)ade flamande, is a beef (or pork) stew popular in Belgium, the Netherlands, and French Flanders.

name: Galette
summary: In French cuisine, a galette (from Norman: gale, 'flat cake') is one of various types of flat round or freeform crusty cakes or pies, or, in the case of a Breton galette (French: Galette bretonne [galɛt bʁətɔn]; Breton: Krampouezhenn gwinizh du), a pancake made with buckwheat flour, usually with a savoury filling.
fun_fact_candidates: One notable variety is the galette des rois (king cake) eaten on the day of Epiphany.

name: Gueuze
summary: Gueuze (French: [ɡøz] ; Dutch: geuze [ˈɣøːzə] ) is a type of lambic, a Belgian beer.
fun_fact_candidates: Due to its lambic blend, gueuze has a different flavor than traditional ales and lagers.
The original, unsweetened version is often referred to as "Oude Gueuze" ("Old Gueuze") and became more popular in the early 2000s.
Traditionally, gueuze, and the lambics from which it is made, have been produced in the area known as Pajottenland and in Brussels.
story_candidates: The name was first seen as the Dutch word 'geuze-bier' in a French text in 1829.
There is some debate on where the word gueuze originated.
One theory is that it originated from geysa (geyser), Old Norse for gush, since, during times of vigorous fermentation, gueuze will spew out of the bunghole of its enclosing oak barrel.
Some American craft breweries have begun blending young and old sour beers, to produce their own versions of the traditional gueuze.

In 2016 Jester King Brewery released a blended, spontaneously fermented beer which it labelled as "Méthode Gueuze." However, the High Council for Artisanal Lambic Beers (HORAL) objected to the name, and the two parties arranged a meeting in Belgium.
Jester King Brewery had no status to represent other American brewers in this meeting, and American brewers were not bound by any agreements made by Jester King's representatives.
HORAL and Jester King agreed that Jester King would use the designation "Méthode Traditionelle" as a style name in the future.
Jester King invited other American brewers to use the Méthode Traditionelle designation for their gueuze-style beers, and proposed a set of standards and a logo for Méthode Traditionelle beers.
Van Honsebrouck St. Louis Gueuze Fond Tradition (5%) St. Louis Premium Gueuze (4.5%)

name: Hochepot
summary: The hochepot (Dutch: hutsepot) is a stew eaten in the Nord-Pas-de-Calais region of France, and in Flanders and Hainaut in Belgium.
fun_fact_candidates: Its origins go back to the Middle Ages and its first known recipes are in the Manuscript of Sion, the oldest treatise on cooking written in French around the 13th century.
story_candidates: Le Viandier de Taillevent, the oldest manuscript of which was written in the 14th century, possesses only one hochepot recipe, with poultry.

name: Lacquemant waffles
sections: Belgian cuisine > Sweet dishes and desserts
summary: A lacquemant is a culinary specialty from the region of Liège, although it was created by Désiré Smidts at the Antwerp Fair, called Sinksenfoor (“Sinksen” is Pentecost in the Antwerpian dialect) where it is still eaten a lot.

name: Lambic
summary: Lambic (English: LAM-bik; French: [lɑ̃bik] ; Dutch: lambiek [lɑmˈbik] ) is a type of beer brewed in the Pajottenland region of Belgium southwest of Brussels since the 13th century.
story_candidates: This beverage is first mentioned in 1794 as allambique.
The initial 'a' was dropped early on so that in an 1811 advertisement it was called lambicq, though it was sometimes referred to as alambic as late as 1829.
Breweries in and around Lembeek, a village near Halle, Belgium, have attempted to associate lambic with that name, including through the legend of local saint Veronus of Lembeek.

name: Liège waffle
summary: Liège waffles are a variety of waffle developed in the Wallonia region of Belgium.
fun_fact_candidates: It is smaller, the dough is a dense and heavy brioche, it contains pearl sugar, and unlike the Brussels waffle, which is traditionally served with toppings, the Liège waffle is traditionally eaten plain.
The Brussels style was introduced in the United States at the 1964 World's Fair, while the Liège version became known outside of Europe decades later.
According to Visit Belgium, the waffle was invented in the 18th century by the chef to the Prince-Bishopric of Liège.

In 2011 Brussels MP Joël Riguelle said the traditional Brussels waffle was in danger of being replaced by the Liège version, which was increasingly being offered in Belgian waffle shops with the toppings traditionally associated with the Brussels waffle.

name: Lokerse paardenworst
summary: The Lokerse paardenworst (Lokeren horse sausage) is a regional product from the Belgian city of Lokeren.
fun_fact_candidates: The Lokerse horse sausage was recognized in 2007 as a Flemish regional product by the Flemish Center for Agro- and Fisheries Marketing (VLAM).
story_candidates: Around the end of the 19th century Lokeren experienced a lot of unemployment and poverty.

name: Mitraillette
summary: A mitraillette (French pronunciation: [mitʁajɛt], lit. 'submachine gun'; Walloon: mitrayète) is a type of sandwich in Belgium commonly served at friteries and cafés.
fun_fact_candidates: It is thought to have originated in Brussels, but is also popular in Flanders, Wallonia, and the Nord region of France, where it is also known as an "Américain" (literally an "American").
story_candidates: After the Brussels bombings in March 2016, images of the sandwich were shared across social media in Belgium and abroad as a sign of friendship and humour.
In December 2020, former Top Chef (France) contestant Jean-Philippe Watteyne opened a pop-up mitraillette restaurant in Mons.
In November 2021, DH Les Sports + reported that a friterie in Etterbeek sells Belgium's longest mitraillette, measuring 130 centimetres (51 in).
In 2025, BetUS.com reported extended queues for a AUS$27 (€16.32) steak mitraillette at the Australian Open.

name: Moules-frites
summary: Moules-frites or moules et frites (French pronunciation: [mul.fʁit]]; Dutch: mosselen-friet) is a main dish of mussels and French fries originating in Northern France and Belgium.
story_candidates: Although moules-frites are popular in many countries, it is thought that the dish originated in Belgium.

It is likely that it was originally created by combining mussels, a popular and cheap foodstuff eaten around the Flemish coast, and fried potatoes, which were commonly eaten around the country in winter when no fish or other food was available.

According to a survey conducted by TNS in 2011, moules-frites was identified as the second-favourite dish in France, receiving a vote of 20 per cent, narrowly losing to magret de canard which received 21 per cent.

name: Open sandwich
summary: An open sandwich, also known as an open-face/open-faced sandwich, bread baser, bread platter or tartine, consists of a single slice of bread or toast with one or more food items on top.
story_candidates: During the start of the Middle Ages, thin slabs of coarse bread called "trenches" (late 15th century English) or, in its French derivative, "trenchers", were used as plates.

A direct precursor to the English sandwich may be found in the Netherlands of the 17th century, where the naturalist John Ray observed that in the taverns, beef hung from the rafters "which they cut into thin slices and eat with bread and butter laying the slices upon the butter".

name: Pain d'épices
summary: Pain d'épices (French: [pɛ̃ depis]) or pain d'épice (French for 'spice bread') is a French cake in the Gateau de Voyage (en.
fun_fact_candidates: Its ingredients, according to Le Dictionnaire de l'Académie française (1694), were "rye flour, honey and spices".
In Alsace, a considerable tradition incorporates a pinch of cinnamon.

name: Paling in 't groen
summary: Paling in 't groen (Dutch) or Anguilles au vert (French) is a Belgian dish, mainly from the Flemish Region along the river Scheldt, between Dendermonde and Antwerp.
fun_fact_candidates: The traditionally home-made meal is also sold fully prepared but still uncooked by some fishmongers' shops or market stalls, and can be enjoyed in specialty restaurants.

learn_more.title: Books about Paling in 't groen (Open Library)

name: Relish
summary: A relish is a cooked and pickled culinary dish made of chopped vegetables, fruits or herbs, typically used as a condiment to enhance a staple.

name: Rijstevlaai
sections: Belgian cuisine > Sweet dishes and desserts
summary: In Belgian and Dutch cuisine, tarte au riz (French: rice pie), rijsttaart(je)/rijstevlaai (Dutch: rice flan), or German: Reisfladen (German: rice flan), is a pie with a filling based on rice pudding.
fun_fact_candidates: It is native to Verviers and popular around the wider region of Eastern Belgium, south-eastern Netherlands and the German region around Aachen.
Traditionally, rijstevlaai are made from unpasteurized cow's milk and stored at room temperature until eaten.
In September 2016, Afsca announced that the pies could be stored at room temperature for up to 12 hours without significant health risks.
Recipes for the tart date back to at least 1604.

name: Samurai sauce
summary: Samurai sauce (French: Sauce samouraï) is a Belgian condiment prepared from mayonnaise, ketchup, and harissa or sambal oelek commonly served with French fries.
fun_fact_candidates: The sauce is also popular and widely used throughout France, and is not to be confused with the also popular Algerian sauce.

name: Sauce américaine
summary: Sauce américaine (pronounced [sos ameʁikɛn]; French for 'American sauce') is a recipe from classic French cookery containing chopped onions, tomatoes, white wine, brandy, salt, cayenne pepper, butter and fish stock.
fun_fact_candidates: It is sometimes incorrectly referred to as sauce armoricaine (pronounced [sos aʁmɔʁikɛn]), but in fact the sauce was invented by a cook from Sète, Hérault, who had worked in the United States.

name: Sauce andalouse
summary: Sauce andalouse is a Belgian condiment commonly served with Belgian fries.
fun_fact_candidates: The sauce is also popular and widely used throughout France and Luxembourg.

name: Shrimp croquettes
summary: Shrimp croquettes, known in Dutch as garnaalkroketten, are a Flemish dish made with grey shrimps (Crangon crangon) caught by local fishermen.
fun_fact_candidates: The traditional method involves cooking immediately on the board itself and peeling by hand.
story_candidates: Shrimps are first mentioned in 12th-century Flemish writings.
In 1850, new docks were built in Ostend.
The tradition of cooking shrimp on the ship started after 1885 to ensure fresh quality.
The 19th century witnessed the growth of the fishing industry.
In Ostend, a circular auction building was established in 1879.
The first shrimp croquette recipe was probably published by Philippe Cauderlier, a chef from Ghent, in his book called Het spaarzame keukenboek (The Thrifty Kitchen Book) in 1914.

name: Sirop de Liège
sections: Belgian cuisine > Sweet dishes and desserts
summary: Sirop de Liège (French for Liège syrup, Luikse siroop in Flemish) is a Belgian jam or jelly-like spread.

learn_more.title: Books about Sirop de Liège (Open Library)

name: Steak frites
summary: Steak frites, meaning "steak [and] chipped potatoes" in French, is a dish consisting of beefsteak accompanied by fried chipped potatoes.
fun_fact_candidates: It is commonly served in Belgian and French brasseries, and is considered by some to be the national dish of Belgium, which claims to be the country of origin.
Steak frites is the subject of a semiotic analysis by the French cultural theorist Roland Barthes in his 1957 work Mythologies.

name: Stoemp
summary: Stoemp is a Flemish dish, found in Belgium, Northern France and the Netherlands, of pureed or mashed potatoes and other root vegetables, and can also include cream, bacon, onion or shallot, herbs, and spices.
story_candidates: Stoemp is traditionally featured alongside fried boudin, fried braadworst, grilled bacon, fried mince or fried eggs.

name: Tartar sauce
summary: Tartar sauce (French: sauce tartare), often spelled tartare sauce in the UK and other Commonwealth countries, is a mayonnaise-based condiment typically containing chopped cornichons or gherkins and capers, along with soft herbs such as tarragon, dill, parsley and chives.
story_candidates: Tartar sauce is named for steak tartare (and thus ultimately named for the Tatars), with which it was commonly served in 19th century France.
Recipes for tartar sauce have been found in English-language cookbooks dating to the mid-19th century, including a recipe in Modern Cookery for Private Families in 1860.
It was also popular in Hungary in the late 19th century.
Tatarska omacka is also very popular in Central and Eastern Europe, in countries like Slovakia, Czechia, Poland, Ukraine etc., where it is a beloved condiment.

name: Tuna salad
summary: Tuna salad is a salad dish consisting of tuna and mayonnaise.
fun_fact_candidates: Pickles, celery, relish, and onion are popular ingredients to add.
story_candidates: The first written reference to tuna salad, in Russia, appeared in 1876, and by 1893, dozens of recipes had been published.
Tuna salad, especially with celery, is similar to chicken salad while also being more convenient (due to the use of canned tuna), a fact that helped its early rise in popularity.
Due to the high nutritional content of tuna salad, it assumed the reputation of a diet food in the 1960s.

name: Vol-au-vent
summary: A vol-au-vent (pronounced [vɔlovɑ̃], French for "fly to the wind", to describe its lightness) is a small hollow case of puff pastry with a filling.
fun_fact_candidates: However, an entremet called petits gâteaux vole au vent is mentioned in François Marin's 1739 cookbook Les Dons de Comus, years before Carême's birth.

name: Waterzooi
summary: Waterzooi (Dutch: [ˈʋaːtərˌzoːi] ) is a soup from Belgium and originating in Flanders.
fun_fact_candidates: It is sometimes called Gentse Waterzooi which refers to the Belgian town of Ghent where it originated.
The original dish is often made of fish, either freshwater or salt, (known as Viszooitje), though today chicken waterzooi (Kippenwaterzooi) is more common.
Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor ate the rich dish, even after suffering from gout.

name: À la zingara
summary: In French cuisine, à la zingara (lit. "gypsy style"), sometimes spelled as à la singara, is a garnish or sauce consisting of chopped ham, tongue, mushrooms and truffles combined with tomato sauce, tarragon and sometimes madeira.
fun_fact_candidates: Gypsy sauce (German: Zigeunersauce) may have originated from à la zingara.
story_candidates: This term was used in the 1903 book Le guide culinaire written by Auguste Escoffier.

In August 2013, a group representing Romani and Sinti peoples called for commercial varieties of the sauce to be renamed, stating that use of the word gypsy is offensive and discriminatory, and has negative connotations.

Authorities in Hanover, Germany, issued an internal memo in October 2013 informing city staffers that they should avoid using the term to describe a type of schnitzel served in the cafeterias of city-run public buildings, instead calling it "Balkan-style" or "Budapest-style".
However, in August 2020, companies such as Knorr replaced the name with "Hungarian-style paprika sauce", citing the recent debates about racism, spurred by the George Floyd protests.

learn_more.title: Books about À la zingara (Open Library)

name: Acarajé
summary: Acarajé (Portuguese: acarajé, pronounced [akaɾaˈʒɛ] ) is a type of fritter made from cowpeas or beans (black-eyed peas) fried in dendê (palm oil).
fun_fact_candidates: This dish is descended from Akara which originated in Yorubaland, from the Yoruba ethnic group inhabiting parts of Nigeria, Benin and Togo.
Acarajé is traditionally encountered in Brazil's northeastern state of Bahia, especially in the city of Salvador.
Acarajé serves as both a religious offering to the gods in the Candomblé religion and as street food.
story_candidates: Today in Bahia, Brazil, most street vendors who serve acarajé are women, known as Baianas do Acarajé, easily recognizable by their all-white cotton dresses and headscarves and caps.
They first appeared in Bahia selling acarajé in the 19th century.

Historically, earnings from the sale of acarajé were used for a variety of reasons including to supplement income and in some cases to buy the freedom of enslaved family members until the abolition of slavery in Brazil in 1888.
Acarajé was featured on the Netflix TV series Street Food volume 2, which focused on Latin American street foods.
The song No Tabuleiro da Baiana, written by Ary Barroso and famously recorded by João Gilberto, Maria Bethânia, Caetano Veloso, and Gilberto Gil, references acarajé, abará, vatapá, and caruru.

name: Acaçá
summary: Acaçá (from Fon language: àkàsà, also known as ẹ̀kọ in Yorùbá language) is a ritual food central to ceremonies of Afro-Brazilian religions, specifically to Candomblé rituals.
fun_fact_candidates: Pai Cido de Osun Eyin stated that "life [...] is sustained, and is renewed with the ritual offering of acaçá." It has at least two variations: a similar dish made of black beans (acaçá de feijão-preto) and a drink (acaçá de leite) also used in Candomblé rituals.
Acaçá is the only ritual food required in Candomblé; it is offered to all the orixás in the Candomblé pantheon.

name: Arabu
summary: Arabu, also known as Mujangué, is an indigenous Brazilian dish from Acre consisting of raw eggs beaten with sugar and manioc flour.
fun_fact_candidates: Traditionally, eggs from the yellow-spotted river turtle were used but eggs from the Brazilian free-range chicken are used nowadays due to environmental reasons.

name: Arroz carreteiro
summary: Arroz carreteiro ("wagoner's rice", in Portuguese) or carreteiro rice is a dish from the Brazilian state of Rio Grande do Sul which has become popular throughout Brazil.
fun_fact_candidates: The dish is traditionally flavoured with garlic, onions, tomato and parsley.
In the Central-West Region and the Northeast of Brazil, arroz carreteiro is also known as maria-isabel and it is prepared with carne-de-sol.
story_candidates: Without refrigeration, the carter was limited to using a dried, salted meat known as carne-de-sol, a type of jerky also known in Rio Grande do Sul as charque.
The traditional arroz carreteiro made with charque in a cast iron pot is one of the main dishes of the state of Rio Grande do Sul.

name: Avoador
sections: Typical and popular desserts > Other popular and traditional desserts
summary: Avoador, often referred to as the generic name biscoito de polvilho and also known as biscoito de vento (air biscuit), peta, or biscoito voador (flying biscuit), is a Brazilian snack food that is typical of Minas Gerais and the cuisine of Central-West Brazil.
fun_fact_candidates: They are popular all throughout Brazil, but especially in the northeast and southeast.
One popular brand is Biscoito Globo sold on the beaches of Rio de Janeiro.
story_candidates: According to historian Luís da Câmara Cascudo, the biscuit was already prepared for rural landowners in 18th century Minas Gerais by farm cooks.

name: Açai bowl
sections: Typical and popular desserts > Other popular and traditional desserts
summary: An açai bowl (açaí na tigela, lit. 'Açaí in the bowl') is a sweet Brazilian snack food from Pará and Amazonas.

name: Baião de dois
summary: Baião de dois (Central Northeastern Portuguese pronunciation: [bajˈɐ̃w ˈdi ˈdojs]) is a dish originating from the Brazilian state of Ceará, typical of the Northeast Region and parts of the North Region, such as Rondônia, Acre, Amazonas and Pará.
fun_fact_candidates: In Paraíba and in Pernambuco, there is a variant called rubacão, a dish that is very popular in the Sertão.
story_candidates: The term gained popularity with the song Baião de Dois, a partnership between the composer from Ceará, Humberto Teixeira, with the "Rei do Baião", from Pernambuco, Luiz Gonzaga, in the mid 20th century.
The cearense origin of the delicacy is attested by the folklorist Câmara Cascudo, citing a reference from 1940, Liceu Cearense, by Gustavo Barroso.

learn_more.title: Books about Baião de dois (Open Library)

name: Bauru (sandwich)
summary: Bauru is a popular Brazilian sandwich.
fun_fact_candidates: The traditional recipe calls for cheese (usually mozzarella) melted in a bain-marie, slices of roast beef, tomato and pickled cucumber in a pão francês with the crumb (the soft inner part) removed.
Many other eateries, though, offer sandwiches named "Bauru" with different combinations of ingredients—for instance, using sliced ham instead of roast beef or sliced bread instead of French bread.
The city of Bauru eventually named the traditional Bauru as the city's official sandwich, codifying the recipe in a municipal law and instituting an official certification program.

name: Beijinho
sections: Typical and popular desserts > Other popular and traditional desserts
summary: Beijinho (Portuguese pronunciation: [bej'ʒĩɲu]; "little kiss" in English), also known as branquinho ("little white one"), is a typical Brazilian birthday party candy prepared with condensed milk, grated desiccated coconut, rolled over caster sugar or grated coconut and frequently topped with a clove.
fun_fact_candidates: Traditionally a single clove is stuck in the top of the candy.
It is believed that Beijinho was originally called "Nun's kiss" and formerly made with almonds, water and sugar.

name: Bife à parmegiana
summary: Bife à parmegiana, or filé à parmegiana, is a Brazilian dish, originally from São Paulo.
fun_fact_candidates: Popularized throughout Brazil, it is a type of fried steak, consisting of a sliced piece of meat, breaded with wheat flour and eggs (egg white), covered with mozzarella cheese, slices of ham and parmesan.
Although it is a dish invented in São Paulo, Brazil, it is often, even in the country itself, mistakenly considered an Italian recipe judging by the name.

learn_more.title: Books about Bife à parmegiana (Open Library)

name: Bobó de camarão
summary: Bobó de camarão (Portuguese pronunciation: [bɔˈbɔ di kɐ̃mɐˈɾɐ̃w]), sometimes referred to as shrimp bobó in English, is a chowder-like Brazilian dish of shrimp in a purée of manioc meal with coconut milk, herbs, ginger, red palm oil, and other ingredients.

learn_more.title: Books about Bobó de camarão (Open Library)

name: Bolinho de chuva
sections: Typical and popular desserts > Other popular and traditional desserts
summary: Bolinho de chuva (European Portuguese pronunciation: [buˈɫiɲu dɨ ˈʃuvɐ]; Brazilian Portuguese pronunciation: [boˈliɲu dʒi ˈʃuvɐ], lit. 'rain pastry') is a dessert both in Portugal and Brazil.
fun_fact_candidates: The popularity of the bolinho de chuva was enhanced in Brazil by the book series Sítio do Picapau Amarelo, where Aunt Nastácia always made them for Pedrinho, Narizinho and the rag doll Emília.

learn_more.title: Books about Bolinho de chuva (Open Library)

name: Bolo de fubá
sections: Typical and popular desserts > Typical cakes (bolos)
summary: Bolo de fubá is a traditional Brazilian cake made with fubá de milho (finely ground maize flour).

name: Bolo de rolo
sections: Typical and popular desserts > Typical cakes (bolos)
summary: Bolo de rolo (Brazilian Portuguese pronunciation: [ˈbolu ˈdi ˈholu]) (lit. 'roll cake') is a cake from the Brazilian state of Pernambuco.
fun_fact_candidates: It is recognized as a national dish in Brazilian law.
story_candidates: The passage of Ordinary Law No. 379/2007 recognized bolo de rolo as intangible heritage of Pernambuco.

learn_more.title: Books about Bolo de rolo (Open Library)

name: Bolo Souza Leão
sections: Typical and popular desserts > Typical cakes (bolos)
summary: Bolo Souza Leão is a cake from the Brazilian state of Pernambuco.
story_candidates: The cake is named after the Sousa Leão family, a notable Brazilian family who owned sugar mills in Northeastern Brazil during the Brazilian sugar cycle, who are credited for its creation.

Another possible origin given by the same source tells that it was created on 18 December 1849 at Engenho Moreno in Moreno, Pernambuco by a member of the Souza Leão family to receive Brazilian emperor Pedro II.

One origin detailed by Brazilian researcher Neide Shinohara and the Diário do Rio tells that the cake was created at Engenho Moreno by Rita de Cássia Souza Leão in 1859 to receive emperor Pedro II and empress Teresa Cristina during one of their trips through Northeastern Brazil.
Brazilian anthropologist Gilberto Freyre met with representatives of the Souza Leão family in the 1960s and convinced them to share the recipe.

learn_more.title: Books about Bolo Souza Leão (Open Library)

name: Brazil nut cake
summary: Brazil nut cake (Portuguese: Bolo de castanha-do-pará) is a cake prepared using Brazil nuts as a primary ingredient.
fun_fact_candidates: Brazil nut cake is a dish in Brazilian cuisine, and it is a common and popular cake in the Amazon region of Bolivia, Brazil and Peru.

learn_more.title: Books about Brazil nut cake (Open Library)

name: Brigadeiro
sections: Typical and popular desserts > Other popular and traditional desserts
summary: Brigadeiro (Brazilian Portuguese pronunciation: [bɾiɡaˈdejɾu]) is a traditional Brazilian dessert.
fun_fact_candidates: The dessert was created by a confectioner, Heloísa Nabuco de Oliveira, to promote the presidential candidacy of Eduardo Gomes.
It is a popular confection throughout the country, especially for festive events.
The mixture may also be served into a small container and eaten with a spoon; this is known as a brigadeiro de colher (literally, "spoon brigadeiro").
In recent years, flavor and coating variations on the traditional chocolate brigadeiros have become popular.
story_candidates: The origin of the name "brigadeiro" is linked to the presidential campaign of Brigadier Eduardo Gomes, UDN candidate for the Presidency of the Republic in 1945.
Heloísa Nabuco de Oliveira, a member of a traditional carioca family who supported the brigadier's candidacy, created a new confection and named it after the candidate.
The doce do brigadeiro (lit. brigadier's candy) became popular, and the name was eventually shortened to just "brigadeiro".
Women at the time would sell brigadeiro in support of the presidential candidate, as it was the first national election in which women were able to vote.
Despite the campaign's popularity, Eduardo Gomes was defeated, and the election was won by then General Eurico Gaspar Dutra.
In the state of Rio Grande do Sul, brigadeiros are most commonly known as negrinhos (literally "little black ones").
One researcher traced its origins back to the 1920s, when condensed milk by Nestlé started being sold in Brazil.

name: Cabeça de galo
summary: Cabeça de galo is a dish from the cuisine of the northeast of Brazil, particularly the states of Pernambuco and Paraíba.

learn_more.title: Books about Cabeça de galo (Open Library)

name: Cachaça
summary: Cachaça ( kə-SHAH-sə; Brazilian Portuguese pronunciation: [kaˈʃasɐ]) is a distilled spirit made from fermented sugarcane juice.
fun_fact_candidates: Also known as pinga, caninha, and other names, it is the most popular spirit in Brazil, and the most popular cane spirit in the world (though almost entirely due to domestic consumption).
Outside Brazil, cachaça is used almost exclusively as an ingredient in tropical drinks, with the caipirinha being the most famous and popular cocktail.
story_candidates: Sugar production was mostly switched from the Madeira islands to Brazil by the Portuguese in the 16th century.
The process dates from 1532, when one of the Portuguese colonists brought the first cuttings of sugar cane to Brazil from Madeira.

In the beginning of the 17th century, the producers of sugar from various European colonies in the Americas used the by-products of sugar, molasses, and scummings as the raw material for the production of alcoholic spirits.

The resulting beverage was known by several names: in British colonies, it was named rum; in France, tafia; in Spain, aguardiente de caña; and in Portugal (Brazil), aguardente da terra, aguardente de cana and later cachaça (locals also call it "Pinga", which translates to drip).
Cachaça's popularity soon exceeded even that of bagaceira, a grape brandy from Portugal.
In response to this, in 1635, the king of Portugal banned production of the spirit, with restrictions reaffirmed and heavy taxation levied in 1659.
This caused the Revolta da Cachaça (Cachaça Rebellion) from 1660 to 1661, which lead to the legalization of cachaça on September 13, 1661, a day that is now celebrated as Cachaça Day.

In 1992, Pró-Cachaça, a program to encourage the expansion of cachaça production, was passed by the Brazilian government, and the following year, the government officially defined cachaça, caninha, and aguardente de cana.
Later, in 2005, the government defined the technical specifications of what qualifies as cachaça, and in 2007, the geographical indication for cachaça was created.
The United States recognized the Brazilian definition for cachaça in 2013.

name: Caipirinha
summary: Caipirinha ( KY-pi-REEN-yə; Brazilian Portuguese pronunciation: [kajpiˈɾĩɲɐ]) is a Brazilian cocktail made with cachaça, sugar, lime, and ice.
fun_fact_candidates: Originating in the state of São Paulo, the drink is prepared by mixing the fruit and the sugar together, then adding the liquor.

Due to its importance and popularity, the caipirinha was declared Brazilian Cultural Heritage in 2003; in 2019, it was considered Intangible Heritage of Rio de Janeiro, despite its origins in Piracicaba, São Paulo.
story_candidates: Although the origin of the drink is unknown, there is a consensus in the academic community that Caipirinha was invented in the interior of São Paulo, Brazil, in 1918.
Some accounts say it came about around 1918 in the region of Alentejo in Portugal, with a popular recipe made with lemon, garlic, and honey, indicated for patients with the Spanish flu.
Another account is that Caipirinha is based on Poncha, an alcoholic drink from Madeira, Portugal.

Once almost unknown outside Brazil, the drink became more popular and more widely available in recent years, in large part due to the rising availability of first-rate brands of cachaça outside Brazil.
The 2001 Brazilian film A Samba for Sherlock fancifully depicts caipirinha as being invented by Doctor Watson as a tonic for Sherlock Holmes to combat the heat of Rio de Janeiro.

name: Cajuzinho
sections: Typical and popular desserts > Other popular and traditional desserts
summary: Cajuzinho Portuguese pronunciation: [kaʒu'zĩɲu] (from caju, "cashew"; literally, "little cashew") is a popular sweet with an almost ubiquitous presences in Brazilian parties.

name: Cajuína
summary: Cajuína (Brazilian Portuguese: [kaˌʒuˈinɐ]) is a non-alcoholic, non-carbonated beverage made of blended cashew apples.
fun_fact_candidates: It is traditional in the northeast region of Brazil, especially in the state of Piauí.
It was invented by writer and pharmacist Rodolfo Teófilo in the 1890s, who sought to find a healthier alternative to alcoholic beverages.
A cashew-flavored carbonated soda is also popularly known as cajuína in Ceará.

name: Canastra cheese
summary: Canastra is a type of cheese from Brazil.
fun_fact_candidates: Its name comes from the region where it is produced, a highland known as Serra da Canastra, located in the southwest region of the Minas Gerais state.
In 2008 the Canastra cheese was deemed to be part of the intangible cultural heritage of Brazil.

name: Canjica (dish)
sections: Typical and popular desserts > Other popular and traditional desserts
summary: Canjica (Portuguese pronunciation: [kɐ̃ˈʒikɐ]), mugunzá ([muɡũˈza]) or mungunzá ([mũɡũˈza]) (these last two are words of African origin) is a Brazilian sweet dish, associated with winter festivals, which in Brazil is in June (Festa Junina).
fun_fact_candidates: Also known as canjicão in some parts of Brazil.
In Colombia and other Latin American countries, one dish similar to canjica cooked corn, known as mazamorra, is widespread in the traditional cuisine.

name: Carne de sol
summary: Carne de sol ([ˈkaʁni dʒi ˈsɔw], Portuguese for "sun meat"), or jabá ([ʒaˈba]) is a dish from Northeastern Brazil.
fun_fact_candidates: Carne de sol is sometimes fried and served as a sandwich, or baked in the oven with cream or, more traditionally, prepared as savory paçoca.
The dish is traditional and typical of the entire northeast region of Brazil, and is served in restaurants all across the country.

learn_more.title: Books about Carne de sol (Open Library)

name: Caruru (food)
summary: Caruru (Brazilian Portuguese: [kaɾu'ɾu]) is a Brazilian food made from okra, onion, shrimp, palm oil and toasted nuts (peanuts and/or cashews).
fun_fact_candidates: It is a typical condiment in the northeastern state of Bahia, where it is commonly eaten with acarajé, an Afro-Brazilian street food made from mashed black-eyed peas formed into a ball and then deep-fried in palm oil.
story_candidates: Guilherme Piso, who lived in Pernambuco (1638–1644), reports the caruru made with medicinal and food herb (and not with okra).

Another account, in 1820, in the Amazon, by Von Martius, mentions the "caruru-açu" during a meal with the natives near the Madeira River, when he experienced "a delicacy of chestnuts pounded with an herb similar to spinach ..." .
During his visit to Africa, at the end of the 18th century, Father Vicente Ferreira Pires called the meal in Daomé "chicken caruru", revealing that the use of oil palm, a palm of African origin.

name: Cauim
summary: Cauim is a traditional alcoholic beverage or beer of the Indigenous peoples in Brazil since pre-Columbian times.
story_candidates: The following description, largely from Jean de Léry's account of his trip to Brazil in the 16th century applies specifically to the Tupinambá natives who lived along the coast of central Brazil.

name: Chouriço doce
summary: Chouriço doce is a blood sausage prepared with pig blood, brown sugar or honey, cashew nuts and spices.
fun_fact_candidates: This is a traditional Portuguese dish from the area of Trás-os-Montes.

name: Cocktails with cachaça
summary: There are many cocktails made with cachaça, the national spirit of Brazil.
fun_fact_candidates: The caipirinha is by far the most popular and internationally well-known, but bartenders have developed other mixed drinks using the spirit.

learn_more.title: Books about Cocktails with cachaça (Open Library)

name: Coconut milk
summary: Coconut milk is a plant milk extracted from the grated pulp of mature coconuts.
fun_fact_candidates: Coconut milk is a traditional food ingredient used in Southeast Asia, Oceania, South Asia, and East Africa.
It is also used for cooking in the Caribbean, Central America, northern parts of South America and West Africa, where coconuts were introduced during the colonial era.
Coconut milk is differentiated into subtypes based on fat content.
A sweetened, processed, coconut milk product from Puerto Rico is also known as cream of coconut, but is distinct from coconut cream and is not interchangeable.
story_candidates: Coconut milk is traditionally made by grating the white inner flesh of mature coconuts and mixing the shredded coconut pulp with a small amount of hot water in order to suspend the fat present in the grated pulp.
Coconut milk is traditionally divided into two grades: coconut cream (or thick coconut milk) and thin coconut milk.
Coconut cream is extracted from the first pressings of grated coconut pulp directly through cheesecloth.
Traditionally prepared coconut milk is utilized immediately after being freshly extracted because it spoils easily when exposed to air.
Coconut milk is also an intermediate step in the traditional wet process methods of producing virgin coconut oil by gradual heating, churning, or fermentation.
In 1943, it was discovered that coconut milk could actively encourage plant growth.
Although there are many factors that attribute coconut milk to plant growth, the main cause is the existence of a cytokinin known as zeatin found in coconut milk.

name: Coxinha
summary: Coxinha ( koh-SHEEN-yə; Portuguese: [koˈʃĩɲɐ], little [chicken] thigh) is a Brazilian snack of Paulista origin which consists of chopped or shredded chicken meat, covered in dough, molded into a shape resembling a teardrop, battered and fried.
story_candidates: Coxinhas were originally made with any part of the chicken, and its traditional shape is meant to resemble a drumstick.
In its modern processed form, it may have originated in Limeira, São Paulo, in the 19th century.

In the book Stories & Recipes, Nadir Cavazin says that the son of Isabel, Princess Imperial of Brazil (1846–1921) and Prince Gaston, Count of Eu, a child who lived in seclusion for having mental problems, had a favorite dish, chicken, but only ate the drumstick.

name: Coxinha de farofa
summary: Coxinha de farofa or coxinha da Lapa is a traditional snack from Lapa.
fun_fact_candidates: Despite being named after coxinha, it is made by covering chicken meat farofa with pastel dough and molded in a shape that resembles a straw.
story_candidates: She was selling pastel during the worship party of Benedict the Moor in Lapa during the 1940s to help funding the construction of a new church for the community.
From there on, the snack became a tradition during the Saint Benedict parties.
It was initially known as "coxinha da dona Glória", but she disapproved of the name.
Rosa Mazur Kugeratski and her daughter Irene copied the recipe and started selling it on her bakery, Panificadora Zeni, thus helping to popularize the snack in the city.
In March 2015, the Prefecture promoted the first Coxinha Party.

learn_more.title: Books about Coxinha de farofa (Open Library)

name: Creme de papaya
sections: Typical and popular desserts > Other popular and traditional desserts
summary: Creme de papaya (Crème de Papaia), also known as papaya mousse, is a Brazilian dessert.
fun_fact_candidates: It was a culinary fad in São Paulo in the 1990s, and became a popular menu item at top restaurants in the city.

learn_more.title: Books about Creme de papaya (Open Library)

name: Curau
sections: Typical and popular desserts > Other popular and traditional desserts
summary: Curau (Portuguese pronunciation: [kuˈɾaw]) is a Brazilian sweet custard-like dessert made from the pressed juice of unripe maize, cooked with milk and sugar.
story_candidates: A giant canjica has been prepared every year since 1999 in the town of Caruaru for the Festa de São João in northeast Brazil; the 2008 issue was 35 meters long and used 4,500 ears of corn.

name: Elevenses
summary: Elevenses () is a short break taken at around 11:00 a.m. to consume a drink or snack.

name: Escondidinho
sections: Main courses or entrées > Additional main course dishes
summary: Escondidinho (from Portuguese: escondido, literally "hidden", plus a diminutive suffix) is a Northeastern Brazilian dish made with carne-de-sol or shredded chicken and topped with a layer of manioc purée.

name: Farofa
summary: Farofa (Brazilian Portuguese: [fa'ɾɔfɐ]) is toasted cassava meal.
fun_fact_candidates: It can be found commercially produced and packaged but can also be prepared at home based on family recipes.

In Brazil, where farofa is particularly popular, typical recipes call for raw cassava flour to be toasted with abundant butter, vegetable oil or olive oil, salt, bacon, onions, garlic, sausage, or olives until golden brown.
In West Africa, a variant of cassava flour known as garri is used in various dishes.

name: Frejon
summary: Frejon (from Portuguese feijão 'beans') is a coconut milk and bean soup which is eaten, especially during Holy Week, by some Christians, mostly Catholics, across the world.
fun_fact_candidates: Countries where frejon is popular include Brazil and Nigeria (especially among Yoruba who returned to Nigeria from Brazil at the abolition of the slave trade, and settled in what is known as the "Brazilian Quarters" in Lagos Island), and Sierra Leone, on Good Friday, or for functions such as weddings.

name: Funge
sections: Main courses or entrées > Additional main course dishes
summary: Funge or fúngi (Angola) or mfundi (Congo - DRC and the Congo Republic) is a traditional African swallow made of cassava flour whisked into boiling water.
fun_fact_candidates: It is also known as bidia (literally "food").
Funge is a traditional staple in Angolan cuisine.
In the Lesser Antilles, a similar food is known as fungi or cou-cou.
In Ghana there are two variations, usually made with ground corn, though the variation known as banku is sometimes made from a mixture of grated cassava and corn.
In Brazilian cuisine, a similar dish made with cassava flour and fish stock is known as pirão.

name: Galinhada
summary: Galinhada is a stew of rice with chicken, which is a typical Brazilian dish in the states of São Paulo, Goiás, Paraná and Minas Gerais.

name: Guaraná (soft drink)
summary: Guaraná is a Brazilian soft drink originating from the guaraná plant.
story_candidates: The processing of the fruit syrup began in Brazil in 1905 by Fara, a physician from the city of Resende, Rio de Janeiro.
A soft drink factory, Guaraná Cyrilla, was launched by F. Diefenthaller in 1906 in Santa Maria, Rio Grande do Sul.
The drink initially was astringent and markedly bitter, and it did not become popular.

The soft drink was created by Pedro Baptista de Andrade, who sold the formula to Antarctica, which then developed a process to eliminate the astringency and bitterness, emphasizing the characteristic flavor and aroma of the fruit, launching Guaraná Champagne Antarctica in 1921.
Guaraná Jesus, another guaraná soft drink, was created accidentally in 1920 by pharmacist Jesus Norberto Gomes, in the state of Maranhão.

Gomes imported a gasification machine to produce a kind of magnesia fluid, a medicine famous at the time, with extracts of 17 ingredients from the Amazon rainforest, including guarana and cinnamon, but the business did not work.
Over time, the taste of the pink drink has become less popular with people, but it remains quite popular in Maranhão, maintaining its original formula.

In Serbia and other Eastern European countries, energy drinks based on guarana are marketed under this name, but without the same sweet flavor as the soda; they have a bitter taste and cardio-accelerating effect.

name: Guaraná Jesus
summary: Guaraná Jesus is a Brazilian soft drink produced by Eduardo Lago, a Coca-Cola bottler based in São Luís.
fun_fact_candidates: The drink is popular within the region, reportedly outselling Coca-Cola, and is made from extracts of the guarana plant, which contains caffeine (sometimes called "guaranine"), theophylline, and theobromine.
The drink is named for Jesus Norberto Gomes, the druggist who formulated the drink in 1920.

name: Ham sandwich
summary: The ham sandwich is a type of sandwich with ham as a primary ingredient.

name: Itubaína
summary: Itubaína is the first Brazilian carbonated soft drink produced by Schincariol which has been produced and distributed nationally since 1954.
fun_fact_candidates: The name is a tribute to the city of Itu, headquarters of the company's first manufacturing plant.
story_candidates: The first flavor of Itubaína, tutti-frutti, was introduced in 1954, and belonged to the former Schincariol.
In 2000, the two-liter version was introduced.
In 2012, a new packaging, the "garrafinha", was launched in 2012, the same year that the manufacturer Schincariol was renamed to Brasil Kirin.
On August 27, 2013, the canned version of Itubaína Retrô was launched, following the "good results" of the brand.
It was initially available in the state of São Paulo and then gradually introduced in other regions of the country.

name: Jerky
summary: Jerky is lean trimmed meat strips which are dehydrated to prevent spoilage and seasoned to varying degrees.
fun_fact_candidates: Many products that are sold as jerky consist of highly processed, chopped, and formed meat rather than traditional sliced whole-muscle meat.

Beef jerky from Inner Mongolia is the most popular jerky product in all of China and is classified into traditional and modern beef jerky by air drying outdoors (hand-made) or thermal drying (large-scale industrial production), respectively.

name: Maniçoba
summary: Maniçoba is a dish in Brazilian cuisine that is from the Brazilian state of Pará located in the Brazilian Amazon.
fun_fact_candidates: Maniçoba is usually eaten during the Círio de Nazaré, a religious festival that takes place in October in the city of Belém.

name: Maria-mole
sections: Typical and popular desserts > Other popular and traditional desserts
summary: Maria-mole (Portuguese pronunciation: [ma'ɾiɐ 'mɔli]; lit. 'limp Mary') is a dessert popular in Brazil that is similar to a marshmallow.
fun_fact_candidates: The dessert was created by Antonio Bergamo, a Brazilian candy maker of Italian descent.

name: Minas cheese
summary: Minas cheese (queijo minas or Portuguese: queijo-de-minas, pronounced [ˈkejʒu (dʒi) ˈmĩnɐs], literally "cheese from Minas") is a type of cheese that has been traditionally produced in the Brazilian state of Minas Gerais.
fun_fact_candidates: It comes in three varieties, named queijos-de-minas frescal (fresh), meia-cura (half-aged) and curado (aged).
Minas cheese is made from cow's milk according to traditional recipes.
It is excellent for cooking, being used for a huge variety of dishes of all types, including pastel de queijo and the famous pão de queijo (cheese bun).
When these two flavors are combined, it is known as Romeu e Julieta, and this combination can be eaten as it is or used in a wide variety of dishes like cake, pie or ice cream.
In December 2024, Minas cheese was recognized by UNESCO as an Intangible cultural heritage.

name: Mocotó
summary: Mocotó (Brazilian Portuguese: [moko'tɔ]) is a Brazilian dish made from cow's feet, stewed with beans and vegetables.
fun_fact_candidates: This dish is also popular in Portuguese cuisine, where it is known as mão de vaca com grão.

name: Moqueca
summary: Moqueca (IPA: [moˈkɛkɐ] or IPA: [muˈkɛkɐ] depending on the dialect, also spelled muqueca) is a Brazilian seafood stew.
fun_fact_candidates: In Manaus, versions based on freshwater fish such as pirarucu and sorubim also prevail.

In Espírito Santo, the subject is taken so seriously that it has become a heritage site – the Ofício das Paneleiras de Goiabeiras, a neighborhood in Vitória, was registered as a cultural asset by the National Historical and Artistic Heritage Institute (Iphan) in 2002.
We do it like the Portuguese: first we hydrate the flour in cold water and only then add the broth.
story_candidates: Moqueca was featured on the Netflix TV series, Street Food volume 2, which focused on Latin American street foods.

name: Mortadella sandwich
summary: The mortadella sandwich (Portuguese: sanduíche de mortadela) is a Brazilian sandwich consisting of mortadella inside pão francês.
fun_fact_candidates: While there are many establishments selling mortadella sandwiches at Mercadão, one of the best known is Bar do Mané, a small restaurant which claims to have made them since opening in 1933.
story_candidates: While the origin of the mortadella sandwich is uncertain, it is believed to have originated in either Hocca Bar or Bar do Mané in the Municipal Market of São Paulo.
The sandwich became incredibly popular after this and was first recognized in a publication on 10 July 1979 after a piece was published by Estadão.

name: Olho de sogra
sections: Typical and popular desserts > Other popular and traditional desserts
summary: Olho de sogra (‘mother-in-law's eye‘ in Portuguese) is a Brazilian candy, consisting of a beijinho candy inside a dried plum (though some recipes include egg yolk).

learn_more.title: Books about Olho de sogra (Open Library)

name: Pamonha
sections: Typical and popular desserts > Other popular and traditional desserts
summary: Pamonha (Portuguese pronunciation: [pɐˈmõɲɐ]) is a traditional Brazilian food.

name: Panela
sections: Typical and popular desserts > Other popular and traditional desserts
summary: Panela (Spanish pronunciation: [paˈnela]) or rapadura (Portuguese pronunciation: [ʁapaˈduɾɐ]) is an unrefined whole cane sugar, typical of Latin America.
fun_fact_candidates: Other traditional NCS include jaggery, which is used in South Asia.

name: Passion fruit mousse
sections: Typical and popular desserts > Other popular and traditional desserts
summary: Passion fruit mousse (Portuguese: mousse de maracujá, sometimes spelled musse) is a passion fruit-flavored variation of mousse from Brazilian cuisine.
fun_fact_candidates: It is usually less aerated than traditional mousses.
story_candidates: In the early 1960s the Brazilian branch of Nestlé was concerned with declining sales of Leite Moça, their condensed milk brand.
Starting in 1961 Nestlé began organized culinary courses and worked with cooking schools to promote Leite Moça.
It was a very successful effort: Nestlé saw an increase in usage, from less than 10% of recipes in courses integrating Leite Moça in 1961, to over 70% of courses using it in some way in 1964.
This affected Brazilian cuisine, especially the desserts: recipes that were once made very similar to their European counterparts were adapted and modified to incorporate condensed milk.
Not long after, passion fruit mousse recipes start to appear; examples can be found as early as 1962.
