name: Allium
summary: Allium is a large genus of monocotyledonous flowering plants with 1112 accepted species, making Allium the largest genus in the family Amaryllidaceae and among the largest plant genera in the world.
fun_fact_candidates: Carl Linnaeus first described the genus Allium in 1753.
story_candidates: When Linnaeus formerly described the genus Allium in his Species Plantarum (1753), there were thirty species with this name.
A. hollandicum 'Purple Sensation' is one of the most popular and has been given an Award of Garden Merit (H4).
Some have been used as traditional medicines.

name: Allium chinense
summary: Allium chinense (also known as Jiaotou, Chinese onion, Chinese scallion, glittering chive, Japanese scallion, Kiangsi scallion, and Oriental onion) is an edible species of Allium, native to China, and cultivated in many other countries.

name: Balut (food)
summary: Balut ( bə-LOOT, BAH-loot; also spelled as balot) is a fertilized developing egg embryo that is boiled or steamed and eaten from the shell.
fun_fact_candidates: It is commonly sold as street food in Southeast Asia, most notably in the Philippines, Cambodia (Khmer: ពងទាកូន, romanized: paung tea kaun), and Vietnam (Vietnamese: trứng vịt lộn, hột vịt lộn), and also occasionally in Thailand (Thai: ไข่ข้าว, romanized: khai khao).
story_candidates: The 2024 horror video game Hapunan has the player taking on the role of Niko, a poor Filipino student who sells balut in Barangay Sak Dudol, where a gang of contract killers is suspected of committing brutal murders during the night.

name: Bamboo
summary: Bamboos are a diverse group of mostly evergreen perennial flowering plants making up the subfamily Bambusoideae of the grass family Poaceae.
story_candidates: In a Chinese legend, the Emperor Yao gave two of his daughters to the future Emperor Shun as a test for his potential to rule.
Shun passed the test of being able to run his household with the two emperor's daughters as wives, and thus Yao made Shun his successor, bypassing his unworthy son.

A bamboo cane is also the weapon of Vietnamese legendary hero, Thánh Gióng, who had grown up immediately and magically since the age of three because of his wish to liberate his land from Ân invaders.
The ancient Vietnamese legend Cây tre trăm đốt (The Hundred-knot Bamboo Tree) tells of a poor, young farmer who fell in love with his landlord's beautiful daughter.
Curious to see such a long bamboo, the landlord was magically joined to the bamboo when he touched it, as the young farmer said the first two magic words.

name: Banana fritter
summary: A banana fritter is a fritter made by deep frying battered banana or plantain in hot cooking oil.
story_candidates: In Suriname, this snack is also known as bakabana (meaning fried banana in Surinamese).

name: Bia hơi
summary: Bia hơi ("fresh beer") is a type of draught beer popular in Vietnam.
fun_fact_candidates: While this lower quality is, in the modern day, deliberate, it has its origins in the 1970s, when the first of these glasses were made rapidly with low-cost materials.

name: Broth
sections: Food in relation to lifestyle > Typical Vietnamese family meal
summary: Broth, also known as bouillon (French pronunciation: [bujɔ̃] ), is a savory liquid made of water in which meat, fish, or vegetables have been simmered for a period of time.
fun_fact_candidates: Dehydrated broth in the form of bouillon cubes was commercialized beginning in the early 20th century.

name: Bun cha
summary: Bún chả (Vietnamese: [ɓun˨˩ ca˧ˀ˦˥]) is a Vietnamese dish of grilled pork and noodles, which is thought to have originated from Hanoi, Vietnam.
fun_fact_candidates: The dish was described in 1959 by Vietnamese food writer Vũ Bằng (1913–1984), who described Hanoi as a town "transfixed by bún chả".
Hanoi's first bún chả restaurant was on Gia Ngư, Hoàn Kiếm District, in Hanoi's Old Quarter.
story_candidates: Bún chả remains very popular in Hanoi and throughout Vietnam.
The origin of the dish is unknown, but one story is that it was created by a grill master in the late 19th or early 20th century in Hanoi.
The Hanoi restaurant Bún Chả Hương Liên became famous after United States President Barack Obama dined there with Chef Anthony Bourdain during his trip to Vietnam in May 2016.

name: Bánh
summary: In Vietnamese, the term bánh (Hanoi: [ɓaʲŋ̟˧˥] or Saigon: [ɓan˧˥], Chữ Nôm: 餅) translates loosely as "cake" or "bread", but refers to a wide variety of prepared foods that can easily be eaten by hands or chopsticks.

name: Bánh bèo
summary: Bánh bèo is a Vietnamese dish originating from Huế, a city in Central Vietnam.
story_candidates: Bánh bèo is associated with Huế, the imperial capital of the Nguyễn dynasty from 1802 to 1945, and is part of the city's tradition of small, delicately presented rice-flour cakes.
Whether the dish itself originated in the imperial court or among commoners is disputed.

Local chef and painter Boi Tran has characterized it as "just a humble snack", while restaurateurs descended from longtime Huế families argue the Nguyễn kings would have appreciated the dish's small portions and refinement.

A separate theory holds that dishes traditionally served on or near banana leaves in Central Vietnam, including bánh bèo, may carry influences from the earlier Cham culture that dominated the region before Vietnamese expansion.

name: Bánh bò
summary: Bánh bò (literally "cow cake" or "crawl cake") is a sweet, chewy sponge cake from Vietnam.
story_candidates: According to the entry for "𤙭" (bò) in Paulus Huỳnh Tịnh Của's 1895 dictionary Đại Nam quấc âm tự vị, the dessert is named for its resemblance to a cow's udder, implying that the name was shortened from bánh vú bò.
However, according to a popular folk etymology, bò refers to how the cake "crawls" up to the rim of the bowl when steamed to completion.

name: Bánh bột chiên
summary: In Vietnamese cuisine, bánh bột chiên are fried rice flour cakes.
fun_fact_candidates: This is a popular after-school snack for young students in southern regions of Vietnam.

learn_more.title: Books about Bánh bột chiên (Open Library)

name: Bánh bột lọc
summary: Bánh bột lọc are small, clear-looking, chewy tapioca dumplings in Vietnamese cuisine that can be eaten as appetizers or small snacks.
fun_fact_candidates: They are said to have originated from Huế, as the city was once the imperial capital of the Nguyễn dynasty and known for having simple, yet sophisticated dishes.

learn_more.title: Books about Bánh bột lọc (Open Library)

name: Bánh canh
summary: Bánh canh (Vietnamese: [ɓaɲ kaɲ]) are thick Vietnamese noodles that can be made from tapioca flour or a mixture of rice and tapioca flour.
fun_fact_candidates: Bánh canh chả cá – the dish includes fish cake and is popular in South Central Vietnam.

name: Bánh chuối
summary: Bánh chuối (literally "banana cake") is a sweet banana cake or bread pudding from Vietnam.

name: Bánh chưng
summary: Bánh chưng, banh chung or chung cake is a traditional Vietnamese dish which is made from glutinous rice, mung beans, pork, and other ingredients.
fun_fact_candidates: According to legend, its origin traces back to Lang Liêu, a prince of the last king of the Sixth Hùng Dynasty.
He earned his place as successor by creating bánh chưng and bánh giầy, which symbolize the earth and the sky, respectively.
Considered an essential element of the family altar on the occasion of Tết, the preparation and consumption of bánh chưng are cherished traditions deeply rooted in Vietnamese culture.
story_candidates: According to the book Lĩnh Nam chích quái (Extraordinary stories of Lĩnh Nam) published in the 14th century, the creation of bánh chưng was credited to Lang Liêu, a prince of the last Sixth Hùng Dynasty of the Hùng dynasty (c. 1712 – 1632 BC).

While other princes tried to find rare and delicious foods from the forest and sea, the eighteenth prince, Lang Liêu, who was the poorest son of the Hùng king, could not afford such luxurious dishes and had to be content with everyday ingredients, such as rice and pork.
In tasting the dishes offered by his son, the Hùng king found bánh chưng and bánh giầy not only delicious but also a fine representation of the respect for ancestors.
Therefore, he decided to cede the throne to Lang Liêu and bánh chưng, bánh giầy became traditional foods during Tết.
Lang Liêu founded the Seventh Hùng dynasty (c. 1631 – 1432 BC).

Wrapped in a green square package, bánh chưng symbolizes the earth, the various ingredients of bánh chưng, which come from all the products of nature, also emphasize the meaning of bánh chưng with Vietnamese people.

Traditionally, bánh chưng requires the preparation of many ingredients, each Vietnamese family that can afford such a preparation begins to make the cake on the 27th or 28th day of the twelfth month of the Vietnamese calendar (tháng Chạp).

Nowadays, the tradition of self-made bánh chưng gradually declines in Vietnam when the size of a typical family is smaller and people do not have enough time for the preparation and making of bánh chưng.

With the shift of bánh chưng making from family to specialized manufacturers, some craft villages became famous for their reputation in making bánh chưng such as Tranh Khúc village or Duyên Hà village both in Thanh Trì, Hanoi.
Each year, on the occasion of the Death anniversary of the Hung Kings, a competition of making bánh chưng and bánh dày is often organized in Hùng Temple, Phú Thọ.

name: Bánh cuốn
summary: Bánh cuốn or bánh quấn (Vietnamese: [ɓǎjŋ̟ kǔən], lit. roll) is a Vietnamese dish originating from Northern Vietnam.

name: Bánh cáy
summary: Bánh cáy is a variety of Vietnamese bánh (translates loosely as "cake" or "bread") made in the Thái Bình Province of northern Vietnam.
fun_fact_candidates: Bánh cáy is traditionally served with tea.

name: Bánh căn
summary: Bánh căn (lit. 'căn cake' or 'small cake') is a pancake-like cake made from rice flour, water, and turmeric.
fun_fact_candidates: It's cooked in a special cast-iron pan or traditional clay pan with round molds and served with toppings like shrimp, pork, and eggs.
It's a popular cake in southern Vietnam, particularly in the provinces of Ninh Thuận (now Khánh Hoà) and Bình Thuận (now Lâm Đồng), as well as in the former city of Đà Lạt.
The origin of bánh căn is unclear, but it is believed to have originated from the Cham people who lived in the province of Ninh Thuận.

name: Bánh cốm
summary: Bánh cốm is a Vietnamese dessert made from rice and mung bean.

name: Bánh cống
summary: Fried shrimp cake (Khmer: នំកំប៉ុង, nom kapong; Vietnamese: bánh cống) is a specialty of Khmer Krom.
fun_fact_candidates: It is thought to be originated in Mỹ Xuyên district, Sóc Trăng province, Southern Vietnam, and over time, the dish has spread across the Mekong Delta, as well as some other localities in Vietnam.

name: Bánh da lợn
summary: Bánh da lợn (or bánh da lợp, bánh da lợt) is a Vietnamese steamed layer cake, mostly popular in Southern Vietnam, made from tapioca starch, rice flour, mashed mung beans, taro, or durian, coconut milk and/or water, and sugar.

learn_more.title: Books about Bánh da lợn (Open Library)

name: Bánh giò
summary: Bánh giò is a Vietnamese steamed pyramid-shaped savory rice cake.
fun_fact_candidates: Bánh giò is thought to be originated in northern Vietnam and now has become a popular street food in all over Vietnam.
It is often kept warm and sold from small carts or stalls, and it is a popular breakfast and snack food.

name: Bánh giầy
summary: Bánh giầy (often mistaken as bánh dầy, bánh dày or bánh giày) is a Vietnamese traditional cake.
story_candidates: The youngest prince, named Lang Liêu, however, loved neither.
One day, toward the end of the year, the emperor met with all his sons.
He told them whoever brought him the most special and unusual food would be made the new emperor.
Almost immediately, the princes left for their homes and started looking for the most delicious food to offer the emperor.
Neither the rough sea nor the violent weather could stop them from looking for the best gifts to please the emperor.
He named the square shaped cake bánh chưng which he made with rice, green beans wrapped in leaves.
On the first day of spring, the princes took the gifts of their labor and love to the emperor.
When it was Lang Liêu's turn to present his gifts, he carried the bánh chưng and his wife carried the bánh dầy to the emperor.
But after tasting all the food brought to court by his sons, the emperor decided that the first prize should be awarded to Lang Liêu.

The emperor then said that his youngest son's gifts were not only the purest, but also the most meaningful, because Lang Liêu had used nothing except rice which was the basic foodstuff of the people to make them.

name: Bánh gối
summary: Bánh gối (Vietnamese for 'pillow bánh'), also known as bánh xếp and bánh quai vạc, is a Vietnamese regional dumpling.
fun_fact_candidates: The dish is a common street food in Vietnam.
story_candidates: Bánh gối is believed to be inspired by the British Cornish pasty or Spanish empanadas and pastel.
Portuguese traders and explorers were the first Europeans to enter Asia in the 1500s, building settlements to test the lucrative spice trade in Goa, India, Malacca and Macau.
Bánh gối originally from Guangdong yau gok; deep-fried jiaozi was introduced to Vietnam before 1954.

name: Bánh hỏi
summary: Bánh hỏi (Vietnamese: [ɓajŋ˧˥ hɔːj˧˩; ɓan˧˥ hɔːj˧˩˧]) is a Vietnamese dish consisting of rice vermicelli woven into intricate bundles and often topped with chopped scallions or garlic chives sauteed in oil, served with a complementary meat dish.
story_candidates: Bánh hỏi originated from the Bình Định Province (now is Gia Lai province) of Vietnam's South Central Coast region.

name: Bánh in
summary: Bánh in (lit. 'seal cake') is a Vietnamese cake from the Huế area given at Tết, Lunar New Year.
fun_fact_candidates: The cake is now quite popular overseas as well and is commonly found all year round in Asian grocery shops worldwide, often in smaller rectangular shaped snack packs.

name: Bánh khoai mì
summary: Bánh khoai mì is a Vietnamese cake made from grated cassava, sugar, coconut milk, and a small amount of salt.
fun_fact_candidates: The Filipino dish, however, differs in its top layer, which is traditionally custard, and in its use of milk as an ingredient.

learn_more.title: Books about Bánh khoai mì (Open Library)

name: Bánh lá
summary: Bánh lá (/bǎɲ lǎ/), literally meaning "leaf cake", is a category of bánh, or Vietnamese cakes, that consist of a parcel of a variety of rice stuffed with some fillings and wrapped in a leaf or leaves.

name: Bánh lọt
summary: Bánh lọt (lit. 'slip through cake') is sweet rice pasta dessert in southern Vietnamese cuisine.
fun_fact_candidates: It is believed to have been introduced to Vietnam from Thailand, where it is called lod chong.

name: Bánh mì
summary: Bánh mì (Vietnamese: [ɓǎjŋ̟ mì]) is a Vietnamese staple food.
fun_fact_candidates: However, a variety of popular fillings are used, like xá xíu (Chinese barbecued pork), xíu mại (Vietnamese minced pork), nem nướng (grilled pork sausage), đậu hũ (tofu), and even ice cream, which is more of a dessert.
The baguette was introduced to Vietnam by the French colonial administration in the mid-19th century, and became a staple food by the early 20th century.
In the 1950s, a distinctly Vietnamese style of sandwich developed in Saigon, becoming a popular street food, also known as bánh mì Sài Gòn ('Saigon sandwich' or 'Saigon-style bánh mì').
Following the Vietnam War, overseas Vietnamese popularized the bánh mì sandwich in countries such as Australia, Canada and the United States.
story_candidates: The word bánh mì, meaning "bread", is attested in Vietnamese as early as the 1830s, in Jean-Louis Taberd's dictionary Dictionarium Latino-Annamiticum.
The French introduced Vietnam to the baguette, along with other baked goods such as pâté chaud, in the 1860s, at the start of their imperialism in Vietnam.
Many sources characterize bánh mì primarily as a French bread tradition adapted in Vietnam, with local fillings added atop the colonial-era baguette base.
Vietnamese vendors layered herbs, pickles, chiles, and meats onto this foundation, producing a distinctive Saigon street-food form by the mid-20th century.
Nguyễn Đình Chiểu mentions the baguette in his 1861 poem "Văn tế nghĩa sĩ Cần Giuộc".
Until the 1950s, sandwiches hewed closely to French tastes, typically a jambon-beurre moistened with a mayonnaise or liver pâté spread.
The 1954 Partition of Vietnam sent over a million migrants from North Vietnam to South Vietnam, transforming Saigon's local cuisine.
Among the migrants were Lê Minh Ngọc and Nguyễn Thị Tịnh, who opened a small bakery named Hòa Mã in District 3.
In 1958, Hòa Mã became one of the first shops to sell bánh mì thịt.
After the Fall of Saigon in 1975, bánh mì sandwiches became a luxury item once again.

name: Bánh mật
summary: Bánh mật is a Vietnamese dessert.

name: Bánh phu thê
summary: Bánh phu thê (lit. 'husband and wife cake') or bánh xu xê, is a Vietnamese dessert made from tapioca flour with mung bean stuffing wrapped in a box made of pandan leaves.
fun_fact_candidates: The dessert was traditionally given by a suitor but is now part of many wedding banquets.
It is traditional for a bridegroom to send bánh phu thê to the bride on the couple's wedding day to symbolize wishes for a happy future.

learn_more.title: Books about Bánh phu thê (Open Library)

name: Bánh pía
summary: Bánh pía (Vietnamese: [ɓaɲ˧˥ fia˧˥]), sometimes written as bánh bía, is a type of Vietnamese bánh (translated loosely as "cake" or "bread").
fun_fact_candidates: A Suzhou style mooncake adapted from Teochew cuisine, called "lâ-piáⁿ" (朥餅, Teochew Peng'im: la⁵ bian²).
In Saigon, the pastry is called bánh bía, while in Sóc Trăng and Vũng Thơm, it is known as bánh pía.
Popular fillings include durian, shredded pork fat, salted egg yolk, mung bean paste, taro and coconut.

name: Bánh rán
summary: Bánh rán is a deep-fried glutinous rice ball Vietnamese dish from northern Vietnam.
fun_fact_candidates: Traditionally, the filling should be separated from the shell so that if one shakes the bánh rán, one can feel the filling rattle against the inside of the shell.
In Southern Vietnam, bánh cam is different from bánh rán as the Northern version is traditionally eaten with a sugary syrup that is poured over the pastry.
Bánh rán is also the Vietnamese translation of the Japanese confection dorayaki, made famous in Vietnam by the manga Doraemon.

name: Bánh rế
summary: Bánh rế, or Rế Cakes, are a Vietnamese street food made from sweet potatoes or cassava.
fun_fact_candidates: They are named after the Vietnamese term “rế”, bamboo baskets, as they look similar.

name: Bánh tráng
summary: Bánh tráng (Vietnamese: [ɓǎɲ ʈ͡ʂǎŋ]), a Vietnamese term (literally, coated bánh), sometimes called rice paper wrappers, rice crepes, rice wafers or nem wrappers, are edible Vietnamese wrappers used in Vietnamese cuisine, primarily in finger foods and appetizers such as Vietnamese nem dishes.

name: Bánh tráng nướng
summary: In Vietnamese cuisine, bánh tráng nướng (lit. 'grilled' or 'roasted bánh tráng') or bánh đa nướng is a type of bánh tráng or grilled rice cracker consumed in Vietnam.
fun_fact_candidates: Traditionally, bánh tráng nướng mè were large, round, thick rice crackers with sesame seeds, which could easily be shattered into smaller pieces.
In recent years, modern street-food versions of bánh tráng nướng have become popular, featuring rice paper grilled with a wide variety of toppings.
They are particularly popular in Đà Lạt, Lâm Đồng province and Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam.

learn_more.title: Books about Bánh tráng nướng (Open Library)

name: Bánh tráng phơi sương
summary: The bánh tráng phơi sương (lit. ''dew-wetted rice paper'') is a special food of Lộc Du, Trảng Bàng District, Tây Ninh Province, Vietnam.

learn_more.title: Books about Bánh tráng phơi sương (Open Library)

name: Bánh tét
summary: Bánh tét is a Vietnamese savoury but sometimes sweetened cake made primarily from glutinous rice, which is rolled in a banana leaf into a thick, log-like cylindrical shape, with a mung bean and pork filling, then boiled.
story_candidates: Bánh tét is a must-have traditional food in Vietnamese Lunar New Year.
During Vietnamese Tết, family members would gather together and enjoy feasting on bánh tét, the central food of this festive Vietnamese holiday to celebrate the coming of spring.

The process of making bánh tét is time-consuming, but a tradition that many families still practice even in this modern society where pre-made bánh tét and bánh chưng are sold virtually in every Vietnamese store.
It is the effort that counts and many choose to spend time with their family to create the holiday treat the traditional way.
The process of making bánh tét is to provide an opportunity for family members to bond and come together to celebrate the holiday spirit.
Bánh tét are traditional to and most popular in central and southern Vietnam.

name: Bánh tẻ
summary: Bánh tẻ (literally "rice cakes" in Vietnamese; also called bánh răng bừa) is a variety of small steamed rice cake in Vietnamese cuisine.
fun_fact_candidates: It is a traditional variety of bánh from the Red River Delta region of northern Vietnam.

name: Bánh xèo
summary: Bánh xèo (Vietnamese: [ɓǎɲ ɕɛ̀w], lit. 'sizzling pancake') is a crispy, stuffed rice crepe popular in Vietnam.
story_candidates: Bánh xèo is a traditional street food in Vietnam.
Bánh xèo has become more popular as more affluent people started to realize its savory taste and new restaurants opening such as Banh Xeo Muoi Xiem and An La Ghien, stated Saigoneers in 2016.

name: Bánh đúc
summary: Bánh đúc is a Vietnamese bánh (cake).

name: Bánh đậu xanh
summary: Bánh đậu xanh (chữ Nôm: 𩚵豆靑, mung bean pastry) is a type of bánh in Vietnamese cuisine.

learn_more.title: Books about Bánh đậu xanh (Open Library)

name: Bì cuốn
summary: In Vietnamese cuisine, bì cuốn are pork and rice rolls.

name: Bò 7 món
summary: Bò bảy món, on menus often "Bò 7 món" (lit. 'seven courses of beef' in Vietnamese) is a set selection of beef dishes in Vietnamese cuisine.

name: Bò nướng lá lốt
summary: Bò nướng lá lốt ("grilled beef in lolot leaf") or thịt bò lá lốt, bò lá lốt is a dish consisting of Vietnamese beef in lolot leaves, which are called "betel" leaves by some English magazines.

learn_more.title: Books about Bò nướng lá lốt (Open Library)

name: Bún bò Huế
summary: Bún bò Huế (pronounced [ɓun˧˥ ɓɔ˧˩ hwe˧˥]) or bún bò (English: ) is a Vietnamese rice noodle (bún) dish with sliced beef (bò), chả lụa, and sometimes pork knuckles.
fun_fact_candidates: The dish originates from Huế, a city in central Vietnam associated with the cooking style of the former royal court.
story_candidates: Bún bò hails from the city of Huế in central Vietnam in the late 1500s and early 1600s, when the city was ruled by the Nguyễn lords.
This classic dish is celebrated for its harmonious blend of spicy, sour, sweet, salty, and umami tastes.

Some say it was historically catered for the royal family and high-ranking officials, and over time, it made its way from the royal kitchens to the street food stalls and homes across central Vietnam.
Others claim of a legend of a young lady named Cô Bún (Ms. Noodles), who perfected noodle making and passed it down to her village of Vân Cù.

learn_more.title: Books about Bún bò Huế (Open Library)

name: Bún mắm
summary: Bún mắm is a Vietnamese vermicelli soup made from fermented fish called mắm, sometimes called "Vietnamese gumbo".

name: Bún riêu
summary: Bún riêu (Vietnamese: [ɓun˧˥ ʐiew˧]) is a traditional Vietnamese soup of clear stock and rice noodles.

name: Bún thịt nướng
summary: Bún thịt nướng (Vietnamese: [ɓǔn tʰìt nɨ̌əŋ], 'rice noodles [with] grilled meat'), which originated from Southern Vietnam, is a popular Vietnamese dish of cold rice noodle topped with grilled pork, fresh herbs like basil and mint, fresh salad, giá (bean sprouts), and chả giò (spring rolls).
fun_fact_candidates: Bún thịt nướng is popular in all regions of Vietnam, alongside Hanoi's bún chả.

learn_more.title: Books about Bún thịt nướng (Open Library)

name: Bún ốc
summary: Bún ốc ("snail vermicelli soup") is a Vietnamese dish originating from Hanoi, Vietnam.
fun_fact_candidates: Roasted or boiled snails (ốc luộc) may be eaten first as an appetizer.

name: Canh chua
summary: Canh chua (Vietnamese: [kajŋ̟ cuə], sour soup) is a Vietnamese sour soup indigenous to the Mekong Delta region of Southern Vietnam (Central Vietnam also have their own canh chua).

name: Cao lầu
summary: Cao lầu is a regional Vietnamese noodle dish, from the city of Hội An, in the central Vietnamese municipality of Da Nang.

name: Caramel
summary: Caramel (, or ) is a range of food ingredients made by heating sugars to high temperatures.
story_candidates: The English word comes from French caramel, borrowed from Spanish caramelo (18th century), itself possibly from Portuguese caramelo.

name: Caramelized pork and eggs
summary: Caramelized pork and eggs or thịt kho tàu is a Vietnamese dish that consists of small pieces of marinated pork and boiled eggs braised in coconut juice.
fun_fact_candidates: Along with being a familiar part of an everyday meal in Vietnam, thịt kho tàu also holds significance as one of the traditional dishes during Tết (Vietnamese New Year).
story_candidates: The first of these narratives recounts the story of Vietnamese fishermen, who would cook large pots of pork stew to bring along with them on their lengthy voyages.
The next narrative is based on the word "tàu" meaning "Chinese".
After the Ming Dynasty was overthrown by the Qing Dynasty, there was a mass exodus of Chinese people to Vietnam.

Thịt kho tàu is believed to have been an interpretation of a dish brought over by the aforementioned Chinese (specifically, the Fujianese) émigrés: tau yu bak (Chinese: 豆油肉), Fujian soy sauce pork and eggs.
Regardless of which of the above three narratives is true, they all share the understanding that thịt kho tàu originated in Vietnam.

learn_more.title: Books about Caramelized pork and eggs (Open Library)

name: Chanh muối
summary: Chanh muối is a salted, pickled lime in Vietnamese cuisine.

name: Ching bo leung
summary: Ching bo leung (Chinese: 清补凉; also spelt ching po leung or qing bu liang; lit. 'refreshing, nourishing, cool') is a sweet, cold dessert soup of Chinese origin, which is commonly served in Cantonese cuisine, Hainanese cuisine and Guangxi cuisine.
fun_fact_candidates: It is a popular dessert in Malaysia and Singapore.
In Singapore it is known as 清汤 ("Cheng Tng" in Hokkien).
It is known as sâm bổ lượng or chè sâm bổ lượng (chè meaning "sweet soup") in Vietnam.
The Chinese form of the drink, ching bo leung, is the most popular in the Cantonese cuisine of Guangdong, Hong Kong, Macau.
It is also popular as a dessert at food & hawker centres in Malaysia and Singapore.
It is sometimes known as luk mei soup (六味汤, lit. 'six flavour soup').

The dish is believed to help "dispel heat" from the body and is popular during the typical hot Hainan weather where there are a prolific number of qing bu liang shops and dessert stands in the tropical island province with varying ingredients and flavours.

learn_more.title: Books about Ching bo leung (Open Library)

name: Cháo lòng
summary: Cháo lòng is a traditional Vietnamese dish consisting of rice porridge (cháo) served with assorted pork offal (lòng).
fun_fact_candidates: It is widely available throughout Vietnam, particularly at street food stalls and casual eateries.

name: Chè
sections: Food in relation to lifestyle > Typical Vietnamese family meal
summary: Chè (Vietnamese pronunciation: [tɕɛ̀]~[cɛ̀]) in traditional Vietnamese cuisine refers to a wide variety of distinct sweet beverages, puddings and desserts.
fun_fact_candidates: Tea is also known as nước chè in the North or more commonly trà in both regions.

name: Chè trôi nước
summary: Chè trôi nước (literally "floating dessert wading in water"; also called chè xôi nước in southern Vietnam, bánh chay in northern Vietnam) is a Vietnamese dessert made of glutinous rice filled with mung bean paste bathed in a sweet clear or brown syrup made of water, sugar, and grated ginger root.
fun_fact_candidates: It is often served during Lunar New Year or, more recently, during the Cold-Eating Festival (March 3 in the Vietnamese calendar).

learn_more.title: Books about Chè trôi nước (Open Library)

name: Chạo tôm
summary: Chạo tôm is a traditional Vietnamese dish that comes from the Huế region of Central Vietnam.

name: Chả
summary: Chả is Vietnamese for "sausage", referring to the Vietnamese types of sausage.

name: Chả giò
summary: Chả giò (Vietnamese: [ca˧ˀ˦˥ zɔ˨˩]), or nem rán (Vietnamese: [neʲm˧ ʐan˧˥]), also known as fried spring roll, is a popular dish in Vietnamese cuisine and usually served as an appetizer in Europe, North America, and Australia, where there are large communities of the Vietnamese diaspora.

name: Coriander
sections: Condiments and sauces > Condiments > Herbs and spices
summary: Coriander (), or Coriandrum sativum, is an annual herb in the family Apiaceae.
fun_fact_candidates: The leaves are known as cilantro () in the US.
All parts of the plant are edible, with the fresh leaves and dried seeds most traditionally used in cooking.
story_candidates: The Ebers Papyrus, an Egyptian text dated around 1550 BCE, mentioned uses of coriander.

name: Corn crab soup
summary: Corn crab soup is a dish found in Chinese cuisine, American Chinese cuisine, and Canadian Chinese cuisine.

learn_more.title: Books about Corn crab soup (Open Library)

name: Curry
sections: Popular dishes > Meat and seafood dishes
summary: Curry (English: /kʌɹiː/, Tamil: [kɐri]) is a dish with a spicy sauce, initially in Indian cuisine, then modified by interchange with the Portuguese, followed by the British, and eventually thoroughly internationalised.
fun_fact_candidates: During the British Raj, Anglo-Indian cuisine developed, leading to Hannah Glasse's 18th century recipe for "currey the India way" in England.
Curry was then spread in the 19th century by indentured Indian sugar workers to the Caribbean and by British traders to Japan.
In China and Korea, curries are based on a commercial curry powder.
In Britain, curry is a popular dish with some types adopted from India and others modified or invented.
story_candidates: Kaṟi is described in a 17th-century Portuguese cookbook, based on trade with Tamil merchants along the Coromandel Coast of southeast India, becoming known as a "spice blend... called kari podi or curry powder".
The first appearance in its anglicised form (spelt currey) was in Hannah Glasse's 1747 book The Art of Cookery Made Plain and Easy.

The cookery writer Pat Chapman noted the similarity of the words Karahi or Kadai, an Indian cooking dish shaped like a wok, without giving evidence. "Curry" is not related to the word cury in The Forme of Cury, a 1390s English cookbook; that term comes from the Middle French word cuire, meaning "to cook".

name: Cơm gà rau thơm
summary: In Vietnamese cuisine, cơm gà rau thơm is a popular chicken and rice dish.

learn_more.title: Books about Cơm gà rau thơm (Open Library)

name: Cơm hến
summary: Cơm hến (baby basket clams rice) is a Vietnamese rice dish originating in Huế.

name: Cơm nắm
summary: Cơm nắm is a Vietnam rice dish of the Northern Vietnam region that is shaped into a roll.

name: Cơm rượu
summary: Cơm rượu (Vietnamese pronunciation: [kəːm ʐɨə̌ˀw]) is a traditional Vietnamese dessert from Southern Vietnam, made from glutinous rice.
fun_fact_candidates: It is also offered on the fifth of May of the lunar calendar, the Vietnamese Mid-year festival.

name: Cơm tấm
summary: Cơm tấm (Vietnamese: [kəːm tə̌m]), also referred as cơm sườn, is a Vietnamese dish made from broken rice, ribs, cucumbers, and pickled carrots, often served with sweet and sour fish sauce.
story_candidates: Cơm Tấm emerged as a popular dish among poor rice farmers in the Mekong Delta.
Since Vietnam's urbanization in the first half of the 20th century, Cơm Tấm became popular across Southern provinces, including Saigon.
In Saigon, which hosted large populations from a range of nations outside Vietnam, food sellers adapted Cơm Tấm to the palates of French, American, Chinese, and Indian customers, among others.
Also, the portion started being served on plates with a fork instead of in traditional bowls with chopsticks.

name: Cốm
summary: Cốm, or simply called green rice, is a flattened and chewy green rice in Vietnamese cuisine.
fun_fact_candidates: It is a popular seasonal dessert across Vietnam, especially in Red River Delta cuisine.
It is traditionally produced at the Cốm Vòng village in Hanoi.
A traditional pastry, bánh cốm (green rice cake), is made using cốm with mung bean filling.
Cốm is often offered to worship ancestors during the Mid-Autumn Festival.

name: Dessert
summary: A dessert is a dish that consists of sweet foods, such as cake, biscuit, ice cream, and possibly a beverage, such as dessert wine or liqueur.
fun_fact_candidates: Desserts commonly conclude a meal as a course in many restaurants, while in some parts of the world, there is no tradition of a dessert course to conclude a meal.
By the 20th century, though, sweet entremets had come to be included among the desserts.
story_candidates: The term "dessert" originated from the French word desservir, meaning "to clear the table", and it referred to the final course of the meal, presented after the table was "cleared" (deservi).

One of the earliest uses of the term in a culinary context is in the Ménagier de Paris (1393), which includes a course of "desserte" in three of the menus, one of which includes sweet pastries and fruits, another of which includes savory frumenty and venison.
In the late 19th century, the word "desserts" also came to refer to the dishes served in the dessert course.

The word "dessert" is most commonly used for this course in Australia, Canada, Ireland, New Zealand, and the United States, while its use exists alongside several synonyms, such as "pudding", "sweets" and "afters" in the United Kingdom and some other Commonwealth countries.
Dried fruit and honey were probably the first sweeteners used in most of the world, but the spread of sugarcane around the world was essential to the development of dessert.

The first apple pie recipe was published in 1381; The earliest documentation of the term cupcake was in "Seventy-five Receipts for Pastry, Cakes, and Sweetmeats" in 1828 in Eliza Leslie's Receipts cookbook.
Frozen foods, including desserts, became very popular starting in the 1920s.

name: Egg coffee
summary: Egg coffee (Vietnamese: Cà phê trứng, (Vietnamese: [kà fe ʈ͡ʂɯ̌ŋ])) is a Vietnamese drink traditionally prepared with egg yolks, sugar, condensed milk and robusta coffee.
fun_fact_candidates: The drink is served in cafes throughout Vietnam, originating in Hanoi.
The son of the café's founder Nguyen Giang claims that his father developed the recipe for the drink when milk was scarce in Vietnam in the late 1940s, replacing milk with egg yolk.

name: Egg soda
summary: Egg soda (Vietnamese: soda sữa hột gà) is a sweet drink made from egg yolk, sweetened condensed milk, and club soda from Southern Vietnam, There are variations of this drink, made with different eggs but most commonly used is a quail egg.

name: Fun guo
summary: Fun guo, or Chaozhou fun guo (潮州粉粿), sometimes spelled fun quor, fun gor, fen guo, Chiu Chow dumpling, Teochew dumpling, or fun kor, is a variety of steamed dumpling from the Chaoshan area of coastal eastern Guangdong, a province in Southern China.

name: Ginseng
summary: Ginseng () is the root of plants in the genus Panax, such as South China ginseng (P. notoginseng), Korean ginseng (P. ginseng), and American ginseng (P. quinquefolius), characterized by the presence of ginsenosides and gintonin.
fun_fact_candidates: Ginseng has been used in the traditional medicine of Korea and China for centuries, although there is no clinical evidence that it has any therapeutic effects.
story_candidates: The first character 人 (pinyin rén; Modern Standard Mandarin pronunciation: [ʐə̌n] or [ɻə̌n]) means "person" and the second character 蔘 (pinyin: shēn; MSM: [ʂə́n]) means "plant root" in a forked shape.
One of the first written texts covering the use of ginseng as a medicinal herb was the Shen Nong Pharmacopoeia, written in China in 196 AD.
In his Compendium of Materia Medica herbal of 1596, Li Shizhen described ginseng as a "superior tonic".
Control over ginseng fields in China and Korea became an issue in the 16th century.

name: Gà nướng sả
summary: In Vietnamese cuisine, Gà nướng sả is grilled chicken with lemon grass (sả).
fun_fact_candidates: Grilled beef and other meats are also popular variations.

learn_more.title: Books about Gà nướng sả (Open Library)

name: Gỏi cuốn
summary: Gỏi cuốn, (Vietnamese pronunciation: [ɣɔj˧˩ kuən˧˦]) nem cuốn, salad roll, summer roll, fresh spring roll, or rice paper roll is a Vietnamese dish traditionally consisting of pork, prawn, vegetables, bún (rice vermicelli), and other ingredients wrapped in bánh tráng (commonly known as rice paper or cold roll).

name: Ham chim peng
summary: Ham chim peng (traditional Chinese: 鹹煎餅; simplified Chinese: 咸煎饼; pinyin: xiánjiānbǐng; Jyutping: haam4 zin1 beng2; lit. 'salty fried pancake'), also known in Singapore and Malaysia as haam ji peng, hum ji peng, among other variations, is a fried Cantonese pastry popular through Southeast Asia.
fun_fact_candidates: The pastry is eaten throughout Southeast Asia, where it is known as Indonesian: kue bantal, and Vietnamese: bánh tiêu, among others.

learn_more.title: Books about Ham chim peng (Open Library)

name: Hủ tiếu
summary: Hủ tiếu or Hủ tíu is a Vietnamese dish eaten in Vietnam as breakfast.
fun_fact_candidates: Hủ tiếu became popular in the 1960s in Southern Vietnam, especially in Saigon.
Hủ tiếu was featured in Master Chef US 2013, where Gordon Ramsay mentioned it being on the top of his list and tasked the contestants to prepare a bowl of hủ tiếu.
The noodle dish also appeared on the TV show Gordon's Great Escape in 2010-2011, where Ramsay tried the noodle dish in Cai Rang floating market in Can Tho.
story_candidates: Hủ tiếu originated with the Teochew from Guangdong province in China who then emigrated to Vietnam.
For the first version of Hủ tiếu, kuay teow, the rice noodles had a softer texture and flat appearance like Phở.

name: Kho (cooking technique)
summary: Kho (Vietnamese: [xɔ˧], chữ Nôm: 𤋹,𪹜, meaning "to simmer", "to braise", or "to stew") is a traditional Vietnamese cooking technique where a protein source, such as beef, pork, poultry, fish, shrimp, or fried tofu, is marinated in fish sauce or soy sauce and spices, such as pepper, garlic, shallot, and ginger, then simmered on medium-low heat in a mixture of nước màu (caramel sauce) and water or a water substitute, such as coconut juice.
story_candidates: Kho was created and became popular within their demographic because it helped them stretch the very limited budgets that they had for food in two distinct ways.
First, kho is a technique where protein sources can be simmered for a long time to make them much more tender.

Even though Vietnam has become a prosperous nation following the Đổi Mới reforms that were initiated in 1986, this economical cooking method continues to be employed by a vast majority of the population.

name: Meat floss
summary: Meat floss, also known as yuk sung or rousong (Chinese: 肉鬆; pinyin: ròusōng; Jyutping: juk6 sung1; Pe̍h-ōe-jī: bah-so͘; Mandarin Chinese: [ɻôʊsʊ́ŋ]), is a dried meat product of Chinese origin, with a light and fluffy texture similar to coarse cotton.
fun_fact_candidates: It is more commonly known as bak hu (Hokkien: 肉拊, Pe̍h-ōe-jī: bah-hú) in Hokkien-influenced regions, such as Southeast Asia and Taiwan.

name: Mì
summary: Mì (mỳ) or mi is a Vietnamese term for noodles.

name: Mì Quảng
summary: Mì Quảng (also written mỳ Quảng, Vietnamese: [mi˨˩ xʷaŋ˧˩˧]), literally "Quảng noodles", is a Vietnamese noodle dish that originated in Quảng Nam Province in central Vietnam.
fun_fact_candidates: It is one of the region's most popular and well recognized food items, and is served on various occasions, like at family parties, death anniversaries, and Tết.
It originated in the Ðà Nẵng and Quảng Nam area and has become available throughout the country, and is eaten at any time of the day.
In August 2024, mì Quảng and phở Nam Định were recognised as part of the national intangible cultural heritage list by the Ministry of Culture, Sports, and Tourism.

name: Mắm cáy
summary: Mắm cáy is a type of fermented fish sauce made from the cáy, a small crab primarily found along the coastal regions of Vietnam.
fun_fact_candidates: Many northern localities in Vietnam are famous for this type of sauce, including Hải Phòng, Hải Dương, Quảng Ninh, Thanh Hoá, Thái Bình, Hà Nam, Phú Thọ... is considered a unique feature of Vietnamese cuisine.

name: Nem nướng
summary: Nem nướng (literally "grilled spring rolls") is Vietnamese grilled pork sausage wrapped around a lemongrass stick and a popular Vietnamese food item, sometimes served as an individual appetizer or snack, mainly served with bánh tráng ["rice paper"] and other herbs and vegetables as a main course.
fun_fact_candidates: Nem nướng is a rustic dish, originating from Ninh Hòa, a northern district of Khánh Hòa Province, about 30km from the coastal city.

name: Nước chấm
sections: Food in relation to lifestyle > Typical Vietnamese family meal
summary: Nước chấm (Vietnamese: [nɯɤk̚˧˥ cʌm˧˥]), or more specifically nước mắm chấm for the fish-sauce version, is a Vietnamese dipping sauce often served as a condiment.

name: Nộm
summary: Nộm or Gỏi (in Southern Vietnam) is the indigenous salad of Vietnamese cuisine.
fun_fact_candidates: Other varieties include bánh đúc nộm salad made with bánh đúc, gỏi bò khô dried beef salad with Vietnamese balm, the popular gỏi đu đủ xanh green papaya salad and gỏi tôm prawn salad and local specialities such as rice-paddy eel salad, gỏi nhệch.

name: Pho
summary: Pho (Vietnamese: phở [fɤ˧˩˧] ) is a Vietnamese soup dish consisting of broth, rice noodles (bánh phở), herbs, and meat – usually beef (phở bò), and sometimes chicken (phở gà).
fun_fact_candidates: Pho is a popular food in Vietnam where it is served in households, street-stalls, and restaurants nationwide.
Residents of the city of Nam Định were the first to create Vietnamese traditional pho.
Pho is a relatively recent addition to the country's cuisine, first appearing in written records in the early 20th century in Northern Vietnam.
After the Vietnam War, refugees popularized it throughout the world.
Influences from both French and Chinese culinary traditions are believed to have contributed to its development in Vietnam, as well as to the etymology of its name.
In 2017, Vietnam made December 12 the "Day of Pho" (Ngày của Phở).
story_candidates: Phở originated in Northern Vietnam in the early 20th century.

While the rice noodles and the spices used in the broth of phở have a connection with Chinese culinary traditions, beef consumption was not widespread among the Vietnamese because they traditionally used water buffaloes for farming.
During French colonial rule (1887–1954), the French introduced pot-au-feu, a slow-cooked beef stew, and the use of beef bones for broth mirrors French consommé techniques.
The modern form emerged between 1900 and 1907 in northern Vietnam, southeast of Hanoi in Nam Định Province, then a substantial textile market.
The traditional home of phở is reputed to be the villages of Vân Cù and Dao Cù (or Giao Cù) in Đông Xuân commune, Nam Trực District, Nam Định Province.

Cultural historian and researcher Trịnh Quang Dũng believes that the popularization and origins of modern pho stemmed from the intersection of several historical and cultural factors in the early 20th century.

The demand for this dish was initially the greatest with workers from the provinces of Yunnan and Guangdong, who had an affinity for the dish due to its similarities to that of their homeland, which eventually popularized and familiarized this dish with the general population.
Hanoi's first two fixed phở stands were a Vietnamese-owned Cát Tường on Cầu Gỗ Street and a Chinese-owned stand in front of Bờ Hồ tram stop.
They were joined in 1918 by two more on Quạt Row and Đồng Row.
Around 1925, a Vân Cù villager named Vạn opened the first "Nam Định style" pho stand in Hanoi.

name: Phá lấu
summary: Phá lấu (Chinese: 拍滷; Pe̍h-ōe-jī: phah-ló̍) is a Vietnamese dish from Ho Chi Minh City, made from pork meat and offal that is braised in a spiced stock of five-spice powder (with curry powder sometimes added).
fun_fact_candidates: A popular variation includes the use of coconut milk in the broth, which imparts a rich and complex flavor to the stew.

name: Prawn cracker
sections: Snacks and starters > Crackers, chips, and crisps
summary: Prawn crackers are deep-fried crackers made from starch and prawn that are popular as snacks and side dishes across Southeast Asia.
fun_fact_candidates: In Indonesia it is known as krupuk udang, while in Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei and southern Thailand it is called keropok udang.

Despite regional differences in terminology, flavouring and customary uses, prawn crackers share a broadly similar method of preparation and form part of a shared culinary tradition across maritime and mainland Southeast Asia.
story_candidates: In the Malay Peninsula, oral tradition attributes the creation of keropok udang (prawn crackers) to the 16th century, when prawn heads left from feasts were repurposed into crackers.
A related preparation, kropeck, is found in the Philippines, where it is thought to have been introduced through early contact with Malay communities prior to Spanish colonisation.

Production in Sa Đéc expanded during the Nguyễn dynasty in the 19th century and the crackers circulated through South China Sea trade routes, showing similarities to varieties elsewhere in Southeast Asia.
Commercial links maintained by Hokkien and Teochew merchants facilitated the movement of these products into Southeast Asia, where they were adapted to local ingredients and preferences.
Across the wider region, the production of prawn crackers formed part of the broader tradition of prawn crackers.
Long-standing trade and cultural networks enabled the circulation of ingredients and methods, linking these local traditions into a wider Southeast Asian pattern of cracker-making.

name: Pâté chaud
summary: Pâté chaud (French: [pate ʃo]), ("hot pastry pie"), also known as patê sô, is a Vietnamese savory puff pastry pie.
fun_fact_candidates: Traditionally, the filling consists of ground pork, but chicken and beef are also now commonly used.
This pie is French-inspired but is now commonly found in bakeries in both Vietnam and the diaspora, much like the Haitian patty.
story_candidates: It was the same usage as in France at the time; for example, Urbain Dubois (1818–1901), in his La Cuisine classique of 1868, describes Pâté-chaud à la Marinière as a moulded meat pie.

name: Rượu cần
summary: Rượu cần (Vietnamese pronunciation: [ʐɯəw˨˩ʔ kɤ̆n˨˩], lit. 'stem liquor' or 'straw liquor') is a fermented rice wine indigenous to several ethnic groups in Vietnam, in areas such as Tây Nguyên or Tây Bắc.

name: Rượu nếp
summary: Rượu nếp (sometimes also called rượu nếp bắc, lit. 'northern glutinous rice wine' or rượu nếp cẩm, lit. 'black glutinous rice wine') is a pudding or drink from northern Vietnam.

name: Rượu thuốc
summary: Rượu thuốc (lit. 'medicinal liquor') or rượu dân tộc (lit. 'traditional liquor') is a kind of Vietnamese distilled liquor (rượu) with herbs and animals, considered by traditional medicine to be good for health.
fun_fact_candidates: In Vietnam, rượu thuốc is widely believed to help drinkers improve their health and virility.

name: Rượu đế
summary: Rượu đế is a distilled liquor from Vietnam, made of either glutinous or non-glutinous rice.
fun_fact_candidates: It is popular in the Mekong Delta region of southwestern Vietnam (its equivalent in northern Vietnam is called rượu quốc lủi).

name: Shaking beef
summary: Shaking beef or bo luc lac (Vietnamese: bò lúc lắc, French: bœuf lôc lac) is a Vietnamese dish that consists of beef that has been cut into small cubes, marinated with fish sauce, soy sauce and oyster sauce, then sauteed in a wok with red onion and bell pepper before being served on a bed of fresh lettuce or watercress with slices of tomato and cucumber.
story_candidates: Shaking beef originated from the sidewalk eateries of Saigon.

When the dish was developed, though it used ingredients brought over by the French, it also followed East and Southeast Asian culinary tradition, which calls for the meat to be cut into bite-sized cubes that can be easily handled with chopsticks and eaten without the use of cutlery.
This detail gives rise to the first possible etymology for the dish.
It was basically named bò lúc lắc because the small, cubed pieces of beef resemble playing dice, which are called hột lúc lắc in Vietnam.

name: Smoked plum
summary: Smoked plum is the smoked fruit of Asian plums, used in East Asian cuisine and medicine.

name: Smoothie
summary: A smoothie is a beverage made by puréeing ingredients in a blender.
story_candidates: Health food stores on the west coast of the United States began selling smoothies with the invention of the electric blender.
The actual term "smoothie" was being used in recipes and trademarks by the mid-1980s.
In the 1960s Steve Kuhnau was inspired by his work as a soda jerk and began experimenting with smoothies.
Kuhnau discovered early success in his smoothie sales and founded Smoothie King.
Smoothie King expanded throughout the United States and pioneered other smoothie businesses.
In the 2000s, consumers began making smoothies at home, in part as an alternative for daily consumption of fruits and vegetables.

name: Snake wine
summary: Snake wine (Chinese: 蛇酒; pinyin: shé-jiǔ; Vietnamese: rượu rắn; Khmer: ស្រាពស់, sra poas; Korean: 뱀술, baemsul) is an alcoholic beverage produced by infusing whole snakes in rice wine or grain alcohol.
fun_fact_candidates: The drink was first recorded to have been consumed in China during the Western Zhou dynasty (c. 1040–770 BC) and thought in folklore to reinvigorate a person according to Traditional Chinese medicine.
It is a traditional drink in much of East Asia and Southeast Asia.
story_candidates: Consumption of snakes and their viscera has long been considered by followers of traditional Chinese medicine to promote health.
Snake bile was offered to the Chinese Ming dynasty statesman Yang Jisheng as treatment for the injuries he suffered in prison circa 1554.

name: Soups in East Asian culture
summary: Soups in East Asian culture are eaten as one of the many main dishes in a meal, or, in some cases served straight with little adornment.
story_candidates: Many soups are consumed as a partial restorative and heavily linked with theories from traditional Chinese medicine.

Popular noodle soups include phở, rice vermicelli (bún bò Huế, bún mọc, bún ốc, Bún riêu cua, bún suông, etc.), mì (mì Quảng in Quảng Nam Province), bánh canh, bánh đa cua (in Hai Phong province), nui, and hủ tiếu.
Hot pot (lẩu) is a popular traditional soup in Vietnam.
Mushroom hot pot was popularized by the Ashima Restaurant chain in Vietnam.

name: Taro cake
summary: Taro cake (traditional Chinese: 芋頭糕; simplified Chinese: 芋头糕; pinyin: yùtóu gāo; Cantonese Yale: wuhtáu gōu) is a Cantonese dish made from the vegetable taro.
story_candidates: In Malaysia and Singapore, it is known as yam cake.

name: Tiết canh
summary: Tiết canh is a Vietnamese dish of raw blood pudding served with cooked meat across Vietnam.
fun_fact_candidates: The most popular is tiết canh vịt, made from freshly killed duck blood, pork and chicken.

name: Tương
summary: Tương (Vietnamese: [tɨəŋ], chữ Hán: 醬) is the name applied to a variety of condiments, a kind of fermented bean paste made from soybean and commonly used in Vietnamese cuisine.
fun_fact_candidates: Originally, the term tương refers to a salty paste made from fermented soybeans, which is popular in vegetarian meals, particularly those prepared and eaten by Vietnamese Buddhist monks.

name: Vietnamese iced coffee
summary: Vietnamese iced coffee (Southern Vietnamese: cà phê sữa đá, lit. 'iced milk coffee'; Northern Vietnamese: cà phê nâu đá, lit. 'iced brown coffee') is a Vietnamese beverage made by pouring hot water through a traditional metal filter, called a phin, containing dark-roast robusta coffee grounds, into a small cup with sweetened condensed milk already in it.
story_candidates: Vietnamese iced coffee has its origins in French colonialism and is believed to be an adaptation of café au lait (coffee with milk).

When compared to traditionally-favored medium-roast Arabica, dark-roast robusta has a greater level of bitterness due to both its darker roast and the fact that it has nearly double the amount of caffeine, which is an inherently bitter compound.

name: Vietnamese lotus tea
summary: Vietnamese lotus tea (trà sen, chè sen, or chè ướp sen) is a traditional Vietnamese scented tea made by infusing green tea with the fragrance of the lotus flower (Nelumbo nucifera).
fun_fact_candidates: It is considered one of the most refined artisanal teas in Vietnam and is often associated with cultural ceremonies, hospitality, and seasonal traditions, particularly in Hanoi.
story_candidates: Artisans often select half-open buds (hàm tiếu), believed to contain the most balanced and concentrated aroma.
Traditional dry-scenting (ướp sen khô) involves repeatedly layering tea leaves with freshly collected lotus anthers over multiple cycles.
An alternative method known as fresh scenting (ướp sen xổi) involves placing tea leaves directly inside a whole lotus flower for a shorter infusion period, typically 24–48 hours.
Lotus tea holds cultural significance in Vietnam as a symbol of refinement, purity, and harmony with nature.
It is often served during formal gatherings, festivals, and as a gesture of hospitality.
The labor-intensive traditional production methods, especially those associated with West Lake, contribute to its reputation as one of Vietnam's most prestigious teas.

name: Vietnamese wine
summary: Vietnamese wine is wine produced in Vietnam.
fun_fact_candidates: The area was first cultivated for viticulture during the French colonial rule of the region in the late 19th century.
The late 20th century saw a renewed focus on the development of Vitis vinifera with the assistance of flying winemakers from regions like Australia.

In 1995, a joint venture with Australian winemakers started an aggressive planting scheme to reintroduce international grape varieties like Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay to land that was until recently littered with landmines left over from the Vietnam War.
story_candidates: Other areas with vineyard plantings include the Central Highland region along the Annamite Range and the southern coastal plain of the Ninh Thuận around Phan Rang – Tháp Chàm where Vietnam's first commercial winery Thien Thai Winery is located.

name: Xôi
summary: Xôi (Vietnamese pronunciation: [soj˧˧]) is a traditional Vietnamese dish made of sticky rice.
story_candidates: As such, it was known as "the sticky rice zone" (vùng thâm canh lúa nếp).

In October 1945, to celebrate the Declaration of Independence of New Vietnam, the people of Hanoi made 100 red xôi trays to offer to the altar of Saint Trần, who was considered the forefather of the Vietnamese ethnic groups.

name: Yogurt
summary: Yogurt (UK: ; US: ; Turkish: yoğurt, pronounced [joˈuɾt]), also spelled yoghurt, is a food produced by bacterial fermentation of milk.
story_candidates: The tradition of fermenting dairy beverages that ultimately gave rise to modern yogurt goes back to millennia, beginning in the domestication of milk-producing animals in Central Asia and the Near East.
In Central Asia, a traditional fermentation process of kumis involves using a horsehide (saba) or stirring the milk in a deep wooden vessel (kubi).
